articles.title: Blue Planet III: Moment Octopus escapes death
articles.summary: The sequence is part of the latest Blue Planet series from Sir David Attenborough.
articles.body:
Filmmakers have captured an octopus's lucky escape after venturing from her normal underwater habitat.

The sequence is part of the latest Blue Planet series from Sir David Attenborough, who has continued to produce nature documentaries into his 101st year.

articles.title: Moment man rescued from sinking car by Australian TV reporter
articles.summary: Journalist Will Murray describes how he and a bystander saved an SUV driver from his vehicle.
articles.body:
A man in a sinking car has been saved by a TV journalist after driving into deep flood water.

Will Murray was at the scene reporting for the Australian Broadcasting Corporation in Morayfield, Queensland, when he saw a vehicle drive past him into the water.

Murray, and a bystander, rushed to help the driver as the SUV sank.

Murray says when it became clear the car was sinking very fast "there was no thinking involved", because the man might have drowned.

"Better that you jump in and give it a crack", Murray tells BBC News.

articles.title: A Lost Schrödinger Manuscript Reveals a Surprising Twist in Quantum Physics
articles.summary: Is the Universe deterministic?
articles.body:
For more than 80 years, a manuscript penned by one of the founders of quantum physics has been gathering dust in an Austrian library.

Now brought to light by physics historian Flavio Del Santo of the University of Geneva, the three-page document is the very soul of brevity – but on it is scrawled a long-lost contribution to one of the most contentious debates in quantum mechanics.

And it offers a surprising insight into what Erwin Schrödinger himself believed about the nature of reality.

Rather than the discomfort with quantum randomness he is often portrayed as espousing, Schrödinger believed that there were aspects of the Universe that couldn't be predicted – a belief he held even before the emergence of quantum theory in the 1920s.

"The strongest plea in favor of indeterminism is older than quantum mechanics," Schrödinger wrote in the unpublished manuscript.

In classical physics, there's no such thing as true randomness. Dice may have nicks and flaws that influence how they roll. Computer random-number generators are usually driven by algorithms. Even coin flips are governed by physical forces that, in theory, could be predicted.

This phenomenon is known as determinism, and it plays an important role in our understanding of the physical Universe, stating that every classical behavior is determined by the conditions that precede it, even if we don't know what all those conditions are.

(The absoluteness of classical determinism has been questioned, but it remains a foundational assumption of classical mechanics.)

But quantum mechanics – as is its wont – marches to the beat of a very different drum.

At the quantum scale, the behavior of particles such as photons and electrons can only be predicted in terms of probabilities. We can calculate the likelihood of a particular outcome with extraordinary precision, but we can't definitively predict what an individual particle will do.

This raises a profound question: Is the Universe fundamentally random, or are there hidden factors that determine particle behavior that quantum mechanics hasn't yet accounted for?

These hypothetical hidden factors are known as hidden variables, and they are what they sound like – unknown properties or conditions that, if we did know them, would allow physicists to predict the quantum behavior of individual particles.

In 1932, mathematician John von Neumann – one of the leading authorities on quantum theory's foundational math – published what was widely interpreted as a mathematical proof that such hidden variables were impossible.

His argument carried considerable weight, and for more than a decade, research into hidden-variable models largely stalled.

Not everyone was convinced. In 1935, mathematician Grete Hermann poked significant holes in von Neumann's reasoning. However, her critique was mostly ignored, and you can probably guess why without much difficulty.

By the mid-1940s, however, two prominent physicists had inadvertently revived the argument for hidden variables – by, ironically, speaking out against them, in agreement with von Neumann.

In May 1943, mathematician and physicist Edmund Taylor Whittaker delivered a lecture arguing that quantum mechanics had finally demolished the classical notion of determinism.

Unlike the apparent randomness of a coin toss, he argued, quantum randomness was genuine, and no amount of additional information could make individual outcomes predictable.

Then, in January 1944, physicist Satyendra Nath Bose made a similar argument in an address to the Indian Science Congress, declaring that "physicists have gained knowledge but lost their faith" in the deterministic laws of nature.

In July 1944, mathematician Henry Piaggio published an article in Nature titled " Collapse of Determinism ," reporting on Bose's arguments. It prompted a flurry of responses from physicists who weren't nearly so convinced that determinism was dead and buried.

Over the ensuing months, the argument blossomed across the journal's pages, with researchers picking apart the supposed impossibility of hidden variables – including Whittaker's seemingly straightforward example involving photons and polarized light.

In his 1943 lecture, Whittaker had proposed a seemingly simple demonstration of why hidden variables couldn't exist, using photons – individual particles of light – passing through a polarizer, a device that filters light according to its orientation.

Quantum mechanics can predict what proportion of photons will pass through the polarizer at any given angle.

But Whittaker argued that if each photon carried a hidden instruction determining whether it would pass through, changing the angle of the polarizer while the photons were in flight would render that instruction useless.

Therefore, he concluded, the outcome couldn't be predetermined by hidden variables.

Enter Schrödinger. Or rather, stay in the wings, Schrödinger.

The physicist had been following the debate, and sometime after November 1944, he penned a response of his own, also titled "Collapse of Determinism" (there were several articles published as part of the debate that used the same title).

In it, he identified a significant flaw in Whittaker's argument.

Whittaker assumed each photon carried a hidden variable with only two possible values, one determining whether it would pass through the polarizer and the other whether it would be reflected.

But Schrödinger pointed out that there was no reason to restrict the hidden variable to just two values. What if it could take any value between zero and one?

He then constructed a mathematical model in which the outcome depended on both the photon's hidden variable and the polarizer's angle.

With the right rules, the model reproduced the probabilities quantum mechanics predicts, without requiring each individual interaction to be random.

There was a second part of the model that was also important. Schrödinger devised a deterministic rule for updating the hidden variable after a photon has passed through the polarizer – which meant his model could be used to reproduce the predictions for subsequent measurements.

Importantly, his aim was not to defend determinism because he necessarily believed in it. He was defending the possibility of determinism against specific claims that it was impossible.

"Experimental evidence + logical deduction can never prove that either the deterministic or the indeterministic view is impossible ," he wrote.

Schrödinger's response, however, never saw the light of day.

Why he never published it remains a mystery, although Del Santo has a possible explanation.

In 1944, physicist Heinrich Pelzer published a similar hidden-variable model, showing that Whittaker's argument didn't hold up. Schrödinger may have learned of Pelzer's work and decided that the point had already been made.

Yet Schrödinger's model went further, providing an explicit mathematical rule for how a photon's hidden variable would change after passing through a polarizer, allowing it to account for successive measurements.

Whatever his reasons, the manuscript remained unpublished, preserved in an Austrian archive until Del Santo brought it to light more than eight decades later.

Although Schrödinger is often portrayed as a champion of determinism, his own philosophical position was rather different.

As early as the 1920s, before modern quantum mechanics had even emerged, Schrödinger had argued that the laws of nature might be fundamentally statistical, rather than governed by an underlying clockwork of perfectly predictable events.

Influenced by physicist Franz Exner, he even described classical determinism as a "philosophic prejudice" and an "a priori belief".

And his unpublished manuscript suggests that his position hadn't fundamentally changed by the 1940s – nor did it later.

Although the "Collapse of Determinism" flurry of the 1940s is largely forgotten today, physicists remain divided by its core positions.

Perhaps what we can learn from Schrödinger's belated contribution is to keep an open mind. In a rather fitting twist, the man who gave us Schrödinger's cat has left us with a question that remains, in its own way, both alive and dead: Is the Universe deterministic… or isn't it?

"Schrödinger … had developed a remarkably strong commitment to indeterminism even before, and independently of, quantum mechanics, which he maintained throughout his career," Del Santo writes .

Models such as Schrödinger's, Del Santo concludes, "serve as proofs of principle against widespread beliefs or alleged impossibility claims, as strikingly illustrated by the case of Schrödinger reconstructed here, but never as expressions of a dogmatic commitment to determinism."

His paper is available on preprint server arXiv .

1º lugar: Gotas de tinta são lançadas por uma impressora sobre o papel em imagem feita com lente de microscópio. — Foto: Ole Bielfeldt/Nikon Small World

Gotas de tinta suspensas no ar, uma aranha coberta de pólen e neurônios dentro do cérebro de um camundongo estão entre as imagens vencedoras de um dos principais concursos de fotografia feita com microscópios .

A edição de 2026 do Nikon Small World recebeu 1.803 imagens de 69 países e premiou 76 registros . O concurso chegou neste ano à sua 52ª edição.

O primeiro lugar ficou com o estudante e fotógrafo experimental alemão Ole Bielfeldt, que registrou gotas de tinta no interior de uma impressora enquanto elas eram lançadas sobre o papel.

Para conseguir a foto, ele adaptou o equipamento e usou uma lente de microscópio.

Em segundo lugar ficou uma imagem de uma aranha-saltadora coberta de pólen, feita por John-Oliver Dum.

O terceiro prêmio foi para Kaelin Wulf e Rachel Flannery, que fotografaram neurônios no cérebro de um camundongo.

articles.title: In Michigan, 3 tribes are on a mission to bring back a fish that disappeared 100 years ago
articles.summary: Tribal nations across the country are trying to restore culturally important species, like the Arctic grayling, while grappling with climate change.
articles.body:
Even when they're young, the characteristic iridescent hues of the Arctic grayling are noticeable at the right angle.

On a brisk morning in September, fish and wildlife biologist Sean Leask counted and measured hundreds of these fish, which were raised at the Grand Traverse Band of Ottawa and Chippewa Indians' streamside rearing facility, located just outside Traverse City in northern Michigan.

"Some of these might be catchable by the end of next year," Leask said. "I don't know what their growth will look like in the wild."

That's because Arctic grayling haven't been seen in Michigan waters for almost a century. By the 1930s, industrial activity like logging and overfishing, along with competition from non-native fish, had decimated their numbers. But three northern Michigan tribes and the state are trying to change that by reintroducing the fish to local waters.

"Our taking care of them and helping them to reestablish their population helps us to reestablish ourselves, our culture, and our traditions," said Tina Frankenberger, the Grand Traverse Band's tribal environmental resiliency lead.

Their work joins broader efforts by tribes around the country to restore native species — from salmon to oysters to condors — that are culturally and economically important, while also strengthening the ecosystems that these species depend on against threats like climate change.

One year into raising and releasing grayling to northern Michigan waterways, biologists with the Michigan tribes are grappling with questions about whether the fish are surviving and how to adapt their efforts to extreme weather. No released grayling have been seen in the wild. Flood conditions and the small number of fish they began with are complicating survey work.

But the tribes remain optimistic that their restoration efforts will improve as they collect more data in the coming years. Biologists think it will be around six to eight years before they can tell if grayling reintroduction has been successful.

"This is an experiment," said Dan Mays, inland policy biologist for the Grand Traverse Band. "We're trying our best."

In the summer and early fall, the Grand Traverse Band raised around 8,000 young grayling and released them into the Boardman-Ottaway River. They're one of three northern Michigan tribes that received grayling eggs from a state hatchery in 2025, along with the Little River Band of Ottawa Indians and the Little Traverse Bay Bands of Odawa Indians. This was the culmination of years of planning plus millions of dollars in combined state , federal , and private funding to restore ecosystems. The eggs for Michigan's reintroduction efforts were sourced from the Chena River in Alaska, a state where Arctic grayling are plentiful and more genetically diverse than the only remaining population in the Lower 48, in Montana's Big Hole River .

Mays is already feeling more optimistic about the number and the size of the grayling that the Grand Traverse Band raised compared to last year, when a power outage at the tribe's rearing facility killed a majority of the grayling.

"Overall, four times as many grayling," he said. "We're also stocking a higher proportion of bigger grayling this year. Greater size, greater survival."

Raising the grayling is one challenge. Tracking the fish to see whether they've survived is another. None of the three northern Michigan tribes have recaptured a grayling yet.

"It's like looking for a needle in a haystack, and the haystack is the size of a river," said Alex Ontkos, an inland fisheries biologist with the Little River Band of Ottawa Indians. Earlier this year, this tribe stocked 391,000 grayling eggs using in-stream incubators on the Manistee River near Kalkaska. Not all of those eggs hatched, with viability rates estimated around 50 to 60 percent, Ontkos said.

Unlike the Grand Traverse Band, the Little River Band let larvae hatch directly into the incubators, grow into tiny fry, then leave the incubator. While biologists observed tens of thousands of fry leaving the incubators, they have yet to see or recapture a grayling.

"I don't think that that's because they're not out there," Ontkos said. "It's just a matter of being in the right place at the right time." The team with the Little River Band will continue to survey for fish this fall.

Being in the right place at the right time has been trickier for another northern Michigan tribe.

Kris Dey, the hatchery manager for the Little Traverse Bay Bands of Odawa Indians, said two years of ice storms and extreme flooding in parts of northern Michigan have made it hard to tell how fish are surviving or growing, as parts of the watershed are still swollen or blocked by storm debris.

"All the places that we scouted for years and prepped and prepared," Dey said, "we have not had a great time getting out into the river and evaluating where they're at and how they're doing."

Looking ahead, Dey worries about how a shifting climate might affect grayling restoration efforts beyond worsening extreme weather. The Arctic fish species thrives in cold waters, and Dey said Michigan waterways will likely trend warmer in the future.

"Trying to plan for a warmer future is very, very difficult," Dey said.

And even after a successful reintroduction, some tribes are grappling with maintaining a species' stability. Thanks to efforts from the St. Croix Chippewa Indians of Wisconsin, lake sturgeon have made a comeback in the Lake Winnebago watershed, but scientists question whether populations can adapt quickly enough to warming winters.

In northern Michigan, biologists said there are ways to adapt their grayling efforts for a changing climate. Dey wants to upgrade the Little Traverse Bay Bands' current egg incubator system to allow the grayling to grow more before release, in hopes of increasing their likelihood of surviving in the wild.

"Climate change and the dramatic weather that we're having may make us do things in a different way," Dey said.

While none of the partner tribes have recaptured a grayling yet, there have been signs of the grayling stocked last year by the team with the Grand Traverse Band. Monitors along the Boardman-Ottaway River have picked up some signals from fish tagged prior to release last year. Leask with the Grand Traverse Band said the signals could've been from a brown trout or an otter with a grayling in its stomach, but he wants to be optimistic.

"I'm hopeful they were a live fish with a tag," Leask said. "It wasn't many, but enough to give you a little hope." The tribe plans to do predation studies next year to find out which animals are eating the grayling.

After counting and measuring, staff with the Grand Traverse Band waded out into the north branch of Boardman-Ottaway River with buckets of grayling. Frankenberger sprinkled some tobacco on the water in an Anishinaabe tradition that helps their ancestors hear prayers more clearly, she said.

After saying her prayer, Frankenberger gently tipped the bucket, then watched the grayling slowly disperse downstream in the Boardman-Ottaway River.

"I think about them reestablishing their connection to this river," she said. "I like to think it'll help rebuild those connections for our people."

This story was originally published by Grist with the headline In Michigan, 3 tribes are on a mission to bring back a fish that disappeared 100 years ago on Oct 21, 2026.

articles.title: Musk pledges $10bn in SpaceX shares for US children: Who really gains?
articles.summary: The pledge, which Trump says will go through tax-friendly ‘Trump accounts’, comes two weeks before the US midterms.
articles.body:
Elon Musk has pledged to give one SpaceX share to every child in the United States next year – a gift that could be worth more than $10bn.

“This will be the first of many,” the world’s richest man wrote on X on Monday.

About 73 million children under 18 live in the US, according to US Census Bureau data.

At Friday’s closing price of $146.03, the pledge would be worth about $10.7bn.

President Donald Trump thanked Musk on his Truth Social platform, and claimed the shares would be given to children “through TRUMP ACCOUNTS”, the tax-friendly investment accounts for children created under his signature tax and spending law last year.

The pledge comes two weeks before the November 3 midterm elections.

Musk is the biggest known donor in the run-up to those elections, having given more than $276m to Republican groups since July.

Musk has not said which children will qualify, when the shares will be handed over, or how.

So how might the giveaway work, and who stands to gain?

SpaceX, the world’s seventh-largest company, began trading on the Nasdaq in June at an initial public offering price of $135 per share. That price has been volatile. SpaceX shares have fallen 35.3 percent since peaking days after the listing.

The shares are currently trading at around $146 a share. Every $1 move in the share price will change the gift’s value by about $73m.

Musk owns 4.8 billion shares in SpaceX outright, according to a filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) in August.

Including unvested awards and stock options, his stake rises to about 6.4 billion shares, or 48.4 percent of the company.

Giving away 73 million shares would reduce his outright holding by about 1.5 percent, barely affecting his control of the company. That’s because his voting power, which is currently about 82 percent because SpaceX has two classes of shares, would fall by only 0.1 percentage points, according to a Bloomberg Opinion calculation.

It would be the largest single gift linked to Trump accounts so far.

Trump said the shares would be held in Trump accounts, and Musk thanked Brad Gerstner, the tech investor behind the accounts, for “helping enable this”.

Nearly 70 million Trump accounts have been opened, one for every child under 18 with a Social Security number, according to the White House. Investments held in Trump accounts can roll up with tax deferred until they are withdrawn when a child turns 18. Alternatively, they can be rolled into a tax-friendly IRA – a retirement account for adults – and continue with the tax-friendly status.

Under Treasury rules published on September 30, donors can now gift individual company stock to children via the accounts. Families and friends making regular contributions to a child’s Trump account are limited to investing low-risk index funds.

Families cannot refuse the shares on behalf of their children and generally cannot sell them for five years, or until the end of the year the child turns 17 if that comes sooner.

Musk cannot sell or trade most of his SpaceX shares until June 2027, the Wall Street Journal reported.

The accounts carry the president’s name, and Trump has tied himself closely to the gift.

He thanked Musk on Truth Social, saying the pledge was “exactly what was envisioned when we created TRUMP ACCOUNTS”.

The White House has presented the accounts as a signature achievement of Trump’s tax law, noting that “every single Democrat voted against” the legislation.

The pledge also marks a public reconciliation. Musk and Trump fell out in 2025 over Trump’s tax-and-spending bill, a rift Trump later called a “little dispute”.

Children will be gaining a share for free, but the gift could also save Musk money.

Donors who give appreciated stock to charity avoid capital gains tax and can usually claim a deduction, the US broadcaster CNBC reported.

As SpaceX’s founder, Musk paid very little for his shares, and selling $10.7bn of them could mean a tax bill of up to about $2.5bn.

It is “a popular practice for particularly high-income taxpayers that would otherwise be paying a high rate”, Will McBride, chief economist at the Tax Foundation, told the broadcaster in May.

Ann Lipton, a law professor at the University of Colorado Boulder, told Inc. magazine that millions of shareholders unable to sell would also have an interest in SpaceX’s success and in “minimising its regulatory burdens”.

For Mitchell Downey, an economist at Stockholm University’s Institute for International Economic Studies who studies political influence in the US, the more striking part of the pledge is what he called “the horseshoe aspect of this” – the idea that right-wing and left-wing policies can curve around and meet.

For decades, progressives have backed the concept of Child Development Accounts, investment accounts for every newborn designed to reduce inequality in wealth, he said. The idea was associated with groups such as the Democracy Collaborative but struggled to gain federal support. Now the idea may become more mainstream as a result of Musk’s gift and Trump accounts.

“It always felt like it might be out of reach,” Downey said. “But I don’t see how Musk’s proposal would be possible without building some infrastructure like this.”

The pledge comes just two weeks before the November 3 midterm elections, which will decide control of the two houses of Congress. All seats in the House of Representatives and one-third of the Senate are up for re-election.

Trump’s approval rating has meanwhile fallen to a record low of 33 percent, according to a Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll, with many political observers expecting to see the Republicans lose seats to the Democratic Party as a result.

Musk, who campaigned with Trump in 2024 and spearheaded the president’s Department of Government Efficiency initiative to reduce the size of the federal workforce, has contributed heavily to Republican candidates in advance of the midterm elections.

Is this legal, and why is it controversial?

Downey said he does not believe the pledge raises legal concerns.

“Individuals are allowed to spend their money in support of a politician,” he told Al Jazeera. “The law only gets violated when either it isn’t publicly reported, or it is part of an explicit and documented quid-pro-quo.”

But he said it does raise ethical concerns, though not ones unique to Musk’s approach.

Those concerns relate to “the outsized role that external donors play in US elections”, Downey said. In his view, they apply much like when someone spends heavily on television advertisements for a candidate.

Downey said the precedent was “hard to assess”.

Because Musk is the richest person in modern history, he said, it is perhaps unsurprising that he is “doing something that involves more money than other very rich people have done”.

He pointed to the Gates Foundation’s spending over the past three decades as “a different type of ‘gift to the public’”. The difference, he said, is that the Gates Foundation focuses funding on health crises in countries in Africa and South Asia – not on voters in the US.

Last year, Gates pledged to “give away virtually all my wealth through the Gates Foundation over the next 20 years to the cause of saving and improving lives around the world”.

articles.title: In Southern California, five rival supercolonies of Argentine ants are engaged in a war; researchers reported 15 million worker ants' deaths in a single war
articles.summary: Millions have died when humans went to war against each other ever since the dawn of humanity.
articles.body: Millions have died when humans went to war against each other ever since the dawn of humanity. While animals are known to have their own rivalries and great wars, one among ants, and at such intensity, is a first. In San Diego, a violent war between five rival ant supercolonies has been raging for decades, killing millions upon millions of them annually, as per a report by IFL Science.Argentine ants: All over the worldThe ants in question are Argentine ants, native to South America. The species (Linepithema humile) is highly territorial and prone to aggression towards other insects, using their antennae and chemical signalling to identify whether others are an outside foe or related friend.Throughout the 19th century, the species was accidentally spread across the world through trans-Atlantic shipping. Ants would hitch a ride on some cargo in South America, then find themselves planted across the world, from Europe to Japan. These different parts of the world were seeded by a small number of ants and their population was much less genetically diverse. They all "smelt" the same to each other, and thus nests treated each other as kin.As they stopped fighting and killing each other, many nests with their own queens merged into one huge cooperative "supercolony" spread across vast areas of land. Decades later, the supercolonies found themselves transplanted into yet another corner of the world, creating a battleground when they came into contact with other supercolonies that had strayed down their own path for generations.A war in CaliforniaAccording to a 2006 paper published in the journal Molecular Ecology, southern California is home to five rival supercolonies of Argentine ants. The most dominant colony controls a 1,000-kilometre-long radius of loosely connected nests along the coasts of California, bordered by at least three of the four smaller colonies, each with their own town-sized enclaves.The scientists from UC San Diego explained that the miles-long borders between the territories were sharp, often divided by just a few metres. When the different groups of ants did come into contact, which they appeared to do regularly, violent clashes erupted.Fights between supercolonies were reported in 40% of the site visits by the researchers, averaging around 15,000 deaths per battle. Over months, the scale of death built up to shocking levels. The researchers estimated that at least 15 million worker ants died in a single border skirmish around one of the smaller colonies near Lake Hodges in north San Diego, over their six-month study.No end in sightWhat's remarkable is that the borders barely moved over the months of the research. They might have shifted back and forth from week to week, but neither side was steadily on winning grounds. The supercolonies were stuck in a war that went on forever, losing massive amounts of life but gaining no new territory.What has shocked the researchers is the similarity between this warfare and that among humans. The stalemate has a striking resemblance to the Western Front of the First World War, where the Allied and Central Powers dug into trenches and ground each other down, with the front line barely moving over the course of years. However, unlike the soldiers of World War I, the supercolony stalemate might not have an end.Writing for Scientific American in 2011, biologist Mark W. Moffett explained that Argentine ants are unusual because they don’t show the “dear enemy effect,” in which territorial animals become less aggressive toward familiar neighbouring rivals than toward unfamiliar strangers after long bouts of violence. Through this effect, a kind of demilitarised zone can eventually emerge along the boundaries where violence does not occur. Under the right circumstances, the two territories can break away from each other, and the killing stops.However, Moffett argued that Argentine ants do not have this privilege. In their native South America, the species will often battle it out over floodplains. Rival colonies will often battle, but the fighting will stop each time the waters rise. The conflict never resolves, so they’re programmed to just keep going, and going, and going.

articles.title: Physicists Trapped a Particle of Antimatter And Kept It Caged For Months
articles.summary: Annihilation free, baby!
articles.body:
The Universe, according to theory at least, should not exist.

Every particle in the Universe has a corresponding antimatter counterpart. Should ever a pair of such particles meet, they would immediately cancel each other out – annihilated in a tiny puff of energy.

Theoretically, the birth of the Universe should have produced equal quantities of particles and antiparticles.

Why the current Universe is so heavily skewed in particles' favor is an enduring mystery – one whose solution remains all the harder to find because of antiparticles' tendency to go and collide with particles.

But an extraordinary effort may have finally tamed one of the biggest tricksters of the antiparticle milieu – the positron, the antimatter counterpart to the ubiquitous electron.

In a cryogenic, superconducting vacuum trap, physicists at Northwestern University in the US successfully kept a single positron for months – a breakthrough that, they say, paves the way to the most rigorous probes yet of particle physics.

"The biggest challenge is to persuade a positron that is ejected from a nucleus in a radioactive decay with a very high energy to slow down enough that we can capture it into our particle trap," Northwestern physicist Gerald Gabrielse, the paper's senior author, told ScienceAlert.

The Universe naturally makes positrons in a variety of ways – cosmic explosions, energetic interactions between particles, and radioactive decay, when an unstable nucleus spits out a positively charged particle otherwise identical to a negatively charged electron.

But the Universe is not kind to positrons. All it has to do to be wiped from existence is encounter a single electron – and electrons are absolutely everywhere.

Physicists have been able to observe positrons since the 1930s, but to study one for any length of time would involve completely isolating it from encountering any other matter.

That's tricky, but not impossible. An electromagnetic trap can keep a single particle hovering in place in a vacuum so that it doesn't accidentally touch another particle.

The problem lies in bringing a particle ejected during the energetic process of radioactive decay to a standstill.

"Most of the positrons that emerge from the source are not successfully slowed and captured," Gabrielse explained. "They end up 'annihilating' with an electron in our apparatus."

The team's solution, spearheaded by Northwestern physicist Tom Myers, had to address both challenges: putting the brakes on the positron, and confining it without bringing it into contact with an electron.

The researchers used a radioactive isotope of sodium as their positron factory, which spits out the antiparticles with an energy of up to around 546 kiloelectronvolts – about 88 percent of the speed of light.

So how do you put the brakes on a relativistic positron?

Well, in this case, the answer is doing the very thing the researchers were ultimately trying to avoid – making it pass through matter. A single crystal of tungsten, to be precise.

The experimental apparatus had three main components: the sodium source, the crystal, and the trap.

First, some of the positrons emitted by the sodium source flew into the tungsten crystal, where their positive electric charge interacted with the negatively charged electrons in the material. Those interactions can excite or ionize atoms, transferring some of the positron's kinetic energy to the crystal.

Most of the positrons don't make it. They smack into electrons, and both are wiped out. But a scant few survive, emerging from the tungsten's surface significantly slowed, hitched to – but not touching – an electron. This is positronium.

In this particular form of positronium, the electron and positron occupy a highly excited quantum state that keeps them relatively far apart, delaying their inevitable annihilation just long enough to transport the positron where it needs to go – straight into the prepared trap.

That trap is also ingenious. A tiny opening, just 640 micrometers wide, allows the positronium to enter, where an electric field strips away the electron, leaving the positron behind.

The device, called a Penning trap, uses a combination of electric and magnetic fields to confine the charged particle without allowing it to touch the walls.

Kept in an extraordinarily good vacuum trap cooled to just 300 millikelvins – a fraction of a degree above absolute zero – the positron can remain isolated from the outside world.

For the researchers, it's a tense experience.

"We turn on our detector and wait," Gabrielse said.

"Eventually we see the electrical signal from a captured positron. We then pull the radioactive source away from the trap to keep any additional positron from loading."

The researchers could keep their captive positron for months. But merely preventing it from annihilating was only the beginning.

They also needed to control its motion with extraordinary precision.

Within the trap's powerful magnetic field, the positron moves in tiny circles – a motion called cyclotron motion. By cooling it to its lowest quantum energy state, the researchers could then use carefully tuned microwaves to nudge it between discrete energy levels, one quantum at a time.

And crucially, they could detect those changes, along with flips in the positron's spin, without disturbing the quantum states being measured.

"I and my research group have been pursuing a one-positron quantum cyclotron for many years, so observing a positron making one-quantum energy jumps was extremely satisfying," Gabrielse said.

"It was also great to see Tom's PhD thesis work culminating in a great success. He had worked very hard."

So why would anyone want to trap and measure a positron in the first place?

Actually, there are a lot of very good reasons – and somewhere near the top of the list is a fundamental principle of physics called CPT symmetry .

CPT stands for charge, parity, and time reversal, three transformations that, when applied together, should leave the fundamental laws of physics unchanged.

One consequence of this principle is that particles and their antimatter counterparts should have some properties that match exactly.

An electron and a positron, for example, each behave a little like a tiny bar magnet, with a property called a magnetic moment. Their magnetic moments should have equal magnitude but opposite sign.

Physicists have already measured the electron's magnetic moment with astonishing precision. Now, thanks to their ability to control a single positron, Gabrielse and his colleagues hope to do the same for its antimatter twin.

"If the magnitudes are the same, it will be the most precise confirmation of the CPT invariance of the Standard Model – the most fundamental mathematical description of physical reality," Gabrielse explained.

The researchers are still in the process of obtaining this measurement, and hope to report a result early next year – although given that this is the best opportunity yet to understand a particle so evasive, it could take longer.

Whatever the measurements reveal, they could provide one of the most stringent tests yet of one of the fundamental principles underpinning modern physics.

And even if the results agree perfectly with theory, that would leave physicists with some very big questions.

"It would deepen the mystery of how the Standard Model can make such precise predictions of what we measure, while being inconsistent with basic features of the Universe," Gabrielse said.

The research has been published in Physical Review Letters .

articles.title: Physicists trap a single antimatter particle for a month
articles.body:
You can't hold antimatter in your hand or even in a regular laboratory apparatus. As soon as antimatter meets matter , the two tend to annihilate each other. This makes studying antimatter tricky. But now physicists have managed to trap a single subatomic particle of the stuff for months at a time in a way that allows them to study its quantum states.

Further investigations using the trap might reveal the secret of why the world around us is made of matter and not antimatter , when things could have presumably gone either way.

Every normal particle of matter has an antimatter counterpart with equal mass but opposite charge. To build their trap, physicists started with atoms of sodium 22, a radioactive isotope with a half-life of about two and a half years. When one of these atoms decays, it emits a positron—the antimatter counterpart of the electron.

"The big challenge is to persuade these positrons to slow down and then capture them," says Gerald Gabrielse, a physicist at Northwestern University, who oversaw the project. The team reported its achievement on Wednesday in Physical Review Letters .

The first step is to send the positrons through the crystal lattice of a sliver of cold tungsten. As the particles go pinballing through the material, they slow down and lose energy. "Every time they bang into something, there's a chance of annihilation, but it doesn't always happen," Gabrielse says. "If they make it to the end, they get popped out."

Next, the physicists steer the positrons along a channel using electromagnetic fields. Eventually the particles end up in a vacuum, just three tenths of a degree Celsius above absolute zero, trapped by an electric field on top and bottom and a magnetic field on the sides. "If you want to hold on to antimatter, you have to hold it in a container without walls," Gabrielse says.

This method allowed the researchers to isolate and study a solitary, lone positron for a month—and could let them do so indefinitely.

The researchers intend to use their trap to make precise measurements of the positron's magnetic moment—basically the strength and orientation of its magnetic field. To do this, they must determine two things: the energy needed to flip the direction of the positron's spin and the energy needed to make it jump from its ground state to its first excited state.

Using a similar trap setup, Gabrielse and his team have already measured the magnetic moment of an electron to a precision of one part in 10 trillion. Taking the equivalent measurement for a positron will allow them to make a crucial comparison. "We're looking to see if they have an exactly opposite magnetic moment," Gabrielse says. That's the prediction of the Standard Model of particle physics. If the two have different values, however, this could help explain why our universe is made of matter instead of antimatter.

Just after the Big Bang, scientists think there were roughly equal amounts of the two. Most of the matter and antimatter must have annihilated, but a small excess of matter was somehow left over to seed the stars and planets we see. The magnetic moment measurement is just one of many realms where physicists are seeking differences between matter and antimatter to account for this profound discrepancy.

"Turn every particle to its antiparticle, look at physics through a mirror (flipping left and right) and press the 'rewind button' to reverse the flow of time," says Roni Harnik, a theoretical physicist at the Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory in Batavia, Ill., who was not involved in the project. "Our most basic theories say that physics stays the same."

If it turns out things are different—that the positron, for instance, has a different magnetic moment than the electron—then we'd have a hint about how matter won out.

"This is an exciting development," Harnik says, "that will enable us to test a basic symmetry."

articles.title: They want your blood
articles.summary: In this week’s Optimizer, we look at why health tech companies are partnering with labs to analyze your blood — and what consumers get from that exchange.
articles.body: This is Optimizer, a weekly newsletter sent from Verge senior reviewer Victoria Song that dissects and discusses the latest gizmos and potions that swear they’re going to change your life. Opt in for Optimizer here. It’s an overcast Saturday morning when I give my 12th vial of blood for testing in six weeks. It’s my 24th this year. At this point, I feel like a pro. I schedule these blood draws first thing in the morning so I don’t get hangry, download the requisition papers ahead of time, avoid strenuous exercise for the 24 hours prior, and make sure to drink a glass of water beforehand so my teeny veins are easier for the phlebotomist to find. In fairness, 12 of the 24 vials were ordered by my doctor to monitor ongoing treatment for a few metabolic issues. Eight were to feed my experimental digital twin. The last four are to test an app called Death Clock, which estimates when you’ll die based on your current health. Currently, the app says I’m going to die at 97 years old on Friday, October 5th, 2085. For greatest accuracy, and to calculate my biological age, Death Clock offers a “free” blood panel with its $69 annual subscription. The app also offers various other optional, upsell panels recommended based on the health history you upload during onboarding. It suggested that I add on tests for thyroid function, heart and artery health, and liver function. On top of the blood panels, the app also recommended I try a continuous glucose monitor, buy a smart scale, buy a blood pressure monitor, get a professional VO2 max evaluation, schedule a liver ultrasound, screen for cervical cancer, start taking daily creatine monohydrate, schedule an annual full-body skin cancer exam, get a baseline coronary CT angiography, consider getting APOE testing for Alzheimer’s risk, and get a colonoscopy. I was getting a vampiric promise of longevity. My blood was the roadmap to a long life. If I did everything the app’s “life lab” proposed, I could get an extra 17 years, dying at the ripe old age of 114 on September 12th, 2102. Even so, watching my blood flow into yet another test tube, I thought of my parents. Blood is more than just a mix of plasma, iron, water, and nutrients. Metaphorically, it’s also a history of the family that came before you — and sometimes, though not always, clues to how they died. [Image: You’re all invited to my death day party on October 5th, 2085. Death Clock is a provocative name, but it’s hardly alone in wanting my blood. Oura and Whoop have already added partnerships with Quest Diagnostics, so their users can hand over their blood too. Google recently announced an integration with Function Health, a startup that makes it easy for people to order these kinds of lab tests. When Apple’s new Health app launches, that too will come with a Quest Diagnostics partnership. Blood is in, and more of these partnerships are undoubtedly on the way. It’s not hard to guess why. Blood contains data — the thing that keeps health tech companies fed. In this age of personalized tech, what could be more personal than the stuff literally flowing through your veins? But as with any highly valuable, highly private data source, the user has to get something equally valuable in return. Right now, that seems to be a vague promise to live longer. “The reality is life is precious, life is short, and we’re all going to die. The question is when, and I think culturally, we are in denial about death,” Brent Franson, founder and CEO of Death Clock, tells me. “Our view is we want to shake people and say, ‘Hey, the only thing that matters most in your life is whether or not you exist,’ and you want to take your health seriously so you can exist as long as possible.” Franson says that to help people understand their own health and the changes they need to make, they have to know what’s going on in their bodies — that’s where the blood comes in. It feels like a hyper-literal take on the idea of looking inside oneself to find the answers to life. It’s an alluring premise, but there’s a limit to what any one person can learn from any quantity of blood. Later in our conversation, Franson acknowledged that the greatest predictor of longevity is socioeconomic status. The rich live longer because they can afford better healthcare — and your blood says nothing about what your income bracket will be. Those limits are sobering to witness firsthand. In April 2021, I got a phone call from my cousin in the middle of the night. My mom was struggling to breathe and had been rushed to the hospital. Something had been wrong with her for a while. Her speech had been slurred for a whole month, and she was struggling with phlegm that just wouldn’t go away. My mom insisted it was a stubborn cold. This cousin, a doctor, suspected my mom had a series of mini strokes and was now suffering from a potential combination of both a stroke and heart attack — a cardiocerebral infarction. In the ER, my mom loudly protested that everyone was worried over nothing. Her father had lived to 101. Her mother was alive and doing well at 94. Her blood, our family blood, was destined for a long life, and we had no history of cardiovascular issues. (Never mind that my uncle had nearly died from a stroke the year prior.) She yelled at the top of her lungs that at 72, she was entirely too young to die. The doctors didn’t find what was wrong with her that night. Over the next few months, we ran her through a gauntlet of tests, many of which involved blood draws and machines of all types. It turned out, my cousin was also wrong. My mom didn’t have a mini stroke and her cardiovascular function was perfectly fine. Instead, she died six months later from spontaneous bulbar amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, which has nothing to do with blood. It was in her body that April, but no blood test would’ve found it. ALS wasn’t in our family history — and as genetic testing later revealed, she didn’t carry the gene for it either. There was nothing she could’ve done to prevent it. The other proposition is that running your blood through a health tech app’s algorithm and AI chatbots will tell you more about yourself. It’s presented as a democratizing move that empowers you to take action outside of the 15 minutes you might get with a doctor — or at the very least, helps you to make the most of an appointment. I’ve uploaded my various blood tests to multiple apps, asking their accompanying AI chatbots to analyze my data. The big-picture interpretations are similar. My tests invariably point to an inflamed but improving liver. I had high cholesterol, but medication seems to be working. My cardiovascular labs have begun to look pretty optimal, according to every app. The combination of good fasting glucose and HbA1c alongside improving but mildly elevated fasting insulin suggests I have “managed” insulin resistance. In other words, I have learned that going to the doctor and addressing my myriad metabolic issues is working. I could have told you that without any of this extra data. [Image: A very weird thing to be eating breakfast and then get this notification. I’ve also learned that doctors, health tech features, and AI can look at the same tests and arrive at different conclusions. For instance, absolutely no one agrees about my most recent fasting insulin. I’ve been told it’s everything from normal to borderline high or high. What should I do? Do I need to do anything? I don’t know, because the advice is all over the place. This type of mixed signaling leads to one of two outcomes. You could become a Bryan Johnson type, where you get 15 vials of blood drawn at once and sell your blood-testing protocol as a product. You could obsess over every tiny change. Or you could be like me and find this thinly disguised datamining expedition mainly repackages things you already know. [Image: Most of these daily habits make sense. Most. “Doctors don’t order these 150 biomarker panels like Function Health, and they don’t do it for a good reason. There’s a high false-positive risk in doing that many tests, especially on somebody who’s asymptomatic for most of the tests. It creates a lot of confusion and annoyance, I think, for existing primary care physicians,” says Franson. When I point out that Death Clock also offers an extensive range of blood tests, he says the difference is the app takes a more middle-of-the-road approach. The app only covers a basic panel in the subscription — the rest are à la carte options depending on an individual’s health needs. Same as a doctor would do, he says. Then what’s the point? “What we want to be tomorrow is a full replacement for primary care as it relates to preventive health,” Franson explains, saying that patients should still go to doctors for scenarios like injuries or surgeries. His vision is to provide a sort of telehealth guidance for everyday lifestyle interventions and routine screening procedures. “It’s kind of a Death Clock on the outside, but it’s a Life Lab once you’re in.” The app does offer some solid advice. Get more steps in. Try to stick to a sleep schedule. Limit alcohol. Eat five servings of fruits and vegetables. Do this consistently for the most benefit. There’s some personalized advice. Mine is centered on getting my liver back to normal. But if the “life lab” is mainly telling me to do more of what I’m doing, to focus on lifestyle interventions — if that’s all any of these health apps do, did they really need my blood? If there’s one thing Franson and I agree on, it’s that we’ll all die someday. Everyone and everything you love will die also. That’s objectively scary and painful. “If we were all a lot healthier, didn’t eat processed food, exercised more, focused on sleep, did less drinking and smoking — the average life expectancy would be higher than it is. There’s no debate about that,” says Franson. “We’re more informed than ever; even so, we’re not smarter than we ever were. We just have much more information … but we don’t have a great solution to the uncomfortable fact that we’re all going to die.” I recognized perhaps a bit of my father in what Franson had to say. He liked control and certainty, and insofar as my father could influence death — the ultimate uncertainty — he did. He took daily walks and did light calisthenics well into his 70s. He obsessed over his diet, took endless supplements, and went to the doctor often. He always boasted that he’d live to 100 years old. He didn’t. Though most people would say dying at 88 is a good run, he spent the last 10 years of his life battling Parkinson’s, eventually losing control of his limbs and forfeiting his memories to dementia. More diseases that can’t be found in your blood. Even so, he refused to cede that his end was out of his hands. It led to a lonely, painful, and drawn-out death. Perhaps where we differ is that I’m less afraid of dying. I’m more worried about prolonged sickness, of holding on just to hold on. Counterintuitively, I’m hoping my blood panels don’t extend my Death Clock estimate further into the future. It’s not that I don’t want to live a long life. I’m just uninterested in a long life without good health. I went into this experiment skeptical, but open to the possibility I could learn something. So far, I’ve mostly decided my blood never held the answer to my real question. How do I live a life that allows me to die well?

articles.title: The simple reason JPMorgan thinks SpaceX will triple: It's going after a $28 trillion market
articles.summary: Analyst Doug Anmuth raised his price target from $240 to $500, making the bull case for SpaceX.
articles.body:
SpaceX ( SPCX ) is on a roll. After reporting earnings for the second time as a public company — turning a profit and showing massive AI revenue — investors are pouring in, driving a 10% gain on Wednesday and stock upgrades from Wall Street.

One analyst note stood out among a strong field: JPMorgan's massive bull thesis. It's common enough for CEO Elon Musk to bet big on himself. But analyst Doug Anmuth laid out another optimistic case, more than doubling his price target to $500 from $240, implying an upside of more than 200% from Wednesday's price.

The reason? In a sentence: "No other company is as well positioned to go after the combined anticipated [total addressable market] of $28T+," Anmuth wrote in a note after earnings.

In other words, SpaceX is going after everything.

Musk's (current) favorite corporate child has already gone beyond rockets and satellites into telecommunications and a complete chip to data center to Grok vertical integration AI, which has overtaken the rest of SpaceX's operations to become its biggest business by revenue. Alone, these businesses would be huge. Together, they approach a quarter of US GDP.

Just imagine if robotaxi and robotics markets get tacked on to that.

In the corporate world, focus often means success — finding the right product, targeting the right customers, and defining the specific value your firm brings. But when you're a giant tech conglomerate, your lane extends to market conquest. Everything is up for grabs, and the name of the game is planting flags. The space race, the AI race, and even, for Musk, the telecom race and supplanting legacy carriers like AT&T ( T ), Verizon ( VZ ), and T-Mobile ( TMUS ).

All of this makes the Tesla ( TSLA ) angle especially interesting. If SpaceX is already on its way to the moon, why not merge with an EV, robotics, and robotaxi company too? The boards of both companies have formed special committees to explore a tie-up. Yet another reason why Musk's enormous ambitions and SpaceX's promising start as a publicly traded company can prompt such lofty projections.

On the company's earnings call Tuesday, Musk said he projects SpaceX's annual recurring revenue by the end of 2027 to fall "somewhere between $500 billion and $1 trillion." This quarter gave us a hint of where things are going, revealing how, in the span of a few months, SpaceX morphed into a new, AI-forward company. The current quarter and the year ahead might very well show another astonishing leap.

Hamza Shaban is a reporter for Yahoo Finance covering markets and the economy. Follow Hamza on X @hshaban .

articles.title: Pupils who designed a badge sent to space meet NASA astronaut
articles.summary: Frank Rubio is set to be in the crew for the Artemis III mission and previously spent a year in space.
articles.body:
Pupils at a school on Anglesey were "very excited" when they met virtually with a NASA astronaut.

Students at Ysgol Cemaes were able to put their questions to Frank Rubio on Wednesday, who is set to be part of the crew for the Artemis III mission .

Rubio also spent more than a year aboard the International Space Station (ISS) after a fault with the spacecraft that was due to bring him and his fellow astronauts back to Earth.

During the virtual session, pupils asked him about his experiences of living and working in space, as well as the challenges and excitement of space travel.

This is not the first time pupils at the primary school have had the chance to speak with astronauts.

Earlier this year, they took part in a project to design a badge that was sent into space, later seeing it float in zero gravity aboard the ISS.

The opportunity was made possible by former pupil Dr Melanie Coathup, a scientist who works closely with astronauts and has helped inspire the school's growing links with the space industry.

Guto Rhys, acting headteacher, said the students were "extremely excited" ahead of the meeting, and had "been looking at videos of life on the ISS and life in space".

The pupils had prepared many questions to ask Rubio.

Harry, 9 and his friend Sofia, 8, were among those listening to the astronaut talk about his experiences.

Harry said: "The most interesting thing I've done today is learning about NASA and Frank Rubio."

The pupils had been busy preparing in the classroom ahead of the meeting, according to Sofia.

She said: "In the school today, we've been learning about Frank Rubio. We learned that if you're sick in space, there are medical kits to help.

"We've been watching some videos about how to brush your teeth and sleep in space."

Lola, 9, was also in the hall for the talk on Wednesday. She was delighted to see Rubio holding a badge that one of the pupils at the school had designed.

"We've been learning about Frank Rubio and that he was supposed to stay in space for six months, but he ended up staying there for a year," she said.

"We got to design a badge to go up to space and it was my cousin who won and her badge got to go up to space."

Speaking to a real astronaut was "very cool" according to Ruby, 10, "because no other schools in Wales will get that experience".

"The most interesting thing that I learned today was that there is a space station up in space," she said.

The school plans to design a new badge very soon, with the plan to send another one up to space next year.

Casas do programa habitacional Minha Casa, Minha Vida, do governo federal — Foto: Semuc/Divulgação

O governo federal e a Prefeitura de Boa Vista entregaram nesta quinta-feira (22) 136 casas a famílias contempladas pelo programa Minha Casa, Minha Vida . Essas são as primeiras moradias entregues aos beneficiários do programa na capital na atual gestão municipal.

As casas ficam em seis conjuntos habitacionais: Capri, Laura Moreira I, Laura Moreira II, Equatorial, Centenário I e Centenário III, todos na zona Oeste de Boa Vista. As casas estão distribuídas da seguinte forma:

Laura Moreira: 40 unidades no Residencial Laura Moreira – módulo 1, e 13 no módulo 2;

Equatorial: 13 unidades no residencial de mesmo nome;

Dr. Airton Rocha: 41 unidades no Residencial Capri;

Centenário: 14 unidades no módulo 1, e 15 no módulo 3.

A cerimônia de entrega das chaves ocorreu no Residencial Laura Moreira I, com a presença do secretário nacional de Habitação do Ministério das Cidades, Augusto Rabelo.

Os contempladas desta vez fazem parte da Faixa 1 do programa, modalidade destinada a famílias de baixa renda. O programa oferece auxílio para facilitar o acesso à casa própria. A seleção da prefeitura englobou famílias com renda bruta mensal de até R$ 2.850 .

Nesta primeira etapa, receberam as moradias famílias que se enquadram nos critérios de prioridade do programa, como mulheres responsáveis pelo sustento da família , famílias com pessoas idosas ou com deficiência , vítimas de violência doméstica , famílias com crianças ou adolescentes entre os dependentes e pessoas em situação de vulnerabilidade social .

Segundo a Prefeitura, as 136 casas desta vez fazem parte de um projeto maior, que prevê a entrega de 999 unidades habitacionais, entre casas e apartamentos, em Boa Vista. A construção dessas unidades havia sido prometido na época da eleição municipal de 2024.

As unidades habitacionais do programa estão sendo construídas em 10 bairros de Boa Vista: Caimbé , Centenário , Cidade Satélite , Dr. Airton Rocha , Equatorial , Jardim Tropical , Jóquei Clube , Laura Moreira , Olímpico e Said Salomão . As inscrições para o programa na capital iniciaram em 2025 .

articles.title: Desmatamento no Acre tem redução de 22% em um ano, aponta Inpe | G1
articles.standfirst: Levantamento aponta que o estado teve 252 km² de áreas desmatadas entre agosto de 2025 e julho de 2026. Na Amazônia Legal, a redução foi de 41,8%, a maior da série histórica.
articles.summary: Levantamento aponta que o estado teve 252 km² de áreas desmatadas entre agosto de 2025 e julho de 2026. Na Amazônia Legal, a redução foi de 41,8%, a maior da série histórica.
articles.body:
📉🌳 O Acre teve uma redução de 22,2% na área desmatada entre agosto de 2025 e julho de 2026, segundo dados do Instituto Nacional de Pesquisas Espaciais ( Inpe ) divulgados na última sexta-feira (16). Conforme o levantamento, o estado passou de 324 km² no período anterior para 252 km² no mais recente.

No entanto, a queda no Acre foi menor que a registrada na Amazônia Legal, onde o desmatamento diminuiu 41,8% e atingiu 3.335 km² , sendo esta a menor área da série histórica do Inpe, iniciada em 1988.

🔎 Os dados fazem parte do Programa de Monitoramento dos Biomas Brasileiros (BiomasBR), por meio do Projeto de Monitoramento do Desmatamento na Amazônia Legal por Satélite (Prodes).

Apesar da redução no Acre, o estado teve o sexto maior índice de desmatamento entre os nove estados da Amazônia Legal no período. O Pará liderou o ranking, com 1.130 km² , seguido por Mato Grosso, com 849 km² , e Amazonas, com 525 km² . Roraima foi a única exceção, com aumento de 0,35%.

O Tocantins teve a maior redução percentual, de 73,3% , seguido pelo Amapá, com 52,9% . Mato Grosso, Amazonas e Pará também registraram quedas superiores a 45%. ( Veja tabela abaixo )

O resultado também mantém a sequência de queda registrada nos últimos anos. Em outubro de 2025, um levantamento anterior do Inpe apontou que o Acre havia registrado cerca de 325 km² de desmatamento entre agosto de 2024 e julho de 2025 , uma redução de 27,6% em relação ao período anterior.

Na época, a taxa era a menor desde 2017. O índice também vinha caindo desde 2021, quando o estado registrou 889 km² de área desmatada.

Essa redução acompanha o endurecimento da fiscalização e do controle sobre o desmatamento ilegal nos últimos anos. Um dos marcos desse movimento foi a retomada, em 2023, do Plano de Ação para Prevenção e Controle do Desmatamento na Amazônia Legal (PPCDAm).

Criado em 2004, o plano reúne ações de diferentes ministérios e esteve por trás da forte queda do desmatamento registrada entre 2004 e 2014 . Planos semelhantes também foram elaborados para os demais biomas, entre eles o Cerrado.

Na prática, essas medidas buscam aumentar o risco de punição para quem desmata ilegalmente. Um dos instrumentos usados são os embargos remotos: áreas desmatadas sem autorização são identificadas por imagens de satélite e bloqueadas sem a necessidade de uma operação em campo.

Com o embargo, o proprietário fica impedido de usar a área e de comercializar o que for produzido nela. Somam-se a isso a atuação dos estados nas ações de controle, o aumento de autuações do Ibama e a maior atenção dos bancos aos dados de desmatamento na concessão de crédito rural.

Assim, propriedades com desmatamento irregular passam a ter mais dificuldade para conseguir financiamento.

Desmatamento no Acre cai mais de 22% em um ano, aponta Inpe — Foto: Flávio Forner/Arquivo pessoal

🚨 A queda na taxa de desmatamento não significa, necessariamente, que a floresta esteja livre de outros danos ambientais. Desmatamento, degradação florestal e queimadas são fenômenos diferentes e não devem ser tratados como um único indicador.

O Prodes calcula a taxa oficial de desmatamento com base na remoção completa da vegetação nativa por corte raso. O sistema também considera situações em que a degradação progressiva provoca a perda completa da cobertura formada pelas copas das árvores.

Já a degradação pode danificar a floresta sem que toda a vegetação seja removida. Queimadas e exploração de madeira, por exemplo, podem comprometer a estrutura da floresta mesmo quando a área não se enquadra nos critérios de desmatamento do levantamento.

Por isso, a taxa anual de desmatamento não corresponde ao número de focos de calor nem à extensão total das áreas queimadas. Cada indicador mede um aspecto diferente dos impactos ambientais.

A estimativa de 2026 considera o período de 1º de agosto de 2025 a 31 de julho de 2026. O levantamento faz parte do Projeto de Monitoramento do Desmatamento na Amazônia Legal por Satélite (Prodes) , do Inpe, responsável pelo cálculo da taxa oficial de desmatamento.

O Prodes utiliza imagens de satélite e uma análise detalhada para identificar a área de vegetação nativa efetivamente suprimida. Por considerar um período anual e exigir um processamento mais aprofundado, o sistema não funciona como um alerta diário para ações de fiscalização.

Essa função cabe ao Sistema de Detecção de Desmatamento em Tempo Real (Deter) , também do Inpe, que identifica alterações na cobertura vegetal e emite alertas para orientar as equipes em campo. Como os sistemas têm objetivos e metodologias diferentes, seus números não são diretamente comparáveis.

Taxa anual de desmatamento não corresponde ao número de focos de calor nem à extensão total das áreas queimadas — Foto: © Nilmar Lage / Greenpeace / Divulgação

Para calcular a taxa da Amazônia Legal, o Inpe analisou 271 dos 516 recortes de imagens que cobrem a região. A seleção priorizou áreas com registros anteriores de desmatamento, alertas do Deter e municípios considerados prioritários para a fiscalização.

Segundo a nota técnica do instituto, os recortes analisados abrangem regiões que concentraram 97,68% do desmatamento registrado pelo Prodes em 2025 e 97,09% das supressões detectadas pelo Deter entre agosto de 2025 e julho de 2026.

No entanto, os números dos dois sistemas não são diretamente comparáveis. A taxa do Prodes costuma, inclusive, ser superior à área apontada pelos alertas do Deter.

articles.title: Two retired aircraft were placed underwater near a Maldives island to create an unusual diving attraction; in 2026, conservation teams began adding coral fragments to help turn the wrecks into a reef
articles.summary: Two retired aircraft that once flew for the Maldives’ first national airline are getting a second life beneath the Indian Ocean, where they are being
articles.body: Two retired aircraft that once flew for the Maldives’ first national airline are getting a second life beneath the Indian Ocean, where they are being transformed from an unusual diving attraction into the foundation of a developing marine habitat. According to the Visit Maldives Corporation’s May 14, 2026, announcement, conservation teams and international media delegates attached coral fragments to specially designed underwater frames and placed them at the Dhoonier Wreck site near Kudagiri Island. The initiative combines the country’s aviation history with efforts to restore coral and diversify marine tourism.The project, known as the Kudagiri Dhoonier Wreck, began in 2025 when two decommissioned Dornier 228 aircraft were submerged in the lagoon beside Kudagiri Picnic Island. The wrecks were intended to create a distinctive underwater attraction for divers and snorkellers, with plans to encourage coral growth and establish an artificial reef over time.From the runway to the seabedThe aircraft once belonged to Air Maldives, the island nation’s first national airline and flag carrier, which ceased operations in 2000. Their placement underwater gives the project a historical dimension, preserving a reminder of the country’s early domestic aviation network in an unusual setting.The name Dhoonier combines “Dhooni”, a Dhivehi word meaning bird, with “Dornier”, the aircraft manufacturer’s name. The symbolism reflects the planes’ transition from machines built for flight to structures resting beneath the water. The project was developed through collaboration between the Housing Development Corporation (HDC), the Maldives Marketing and Public Relations Corporation (MMPRC) and the Maldives Transport and Contracting Company (MTCC). HDC is responsible for maintaining the site.The aircraft were transported to the lagoon by barge, lifted into the water with cranes and guided towards the seabed by scuba divers. Weights were attached to help stabilise them on the sandy lagoon floor, according to a March 2025 report by Manta Media Maldives. The report placed the wreck site at approximately 12 metres below the surface, making it potentially accessible to snorkellers and freedivers as well as scuba divers, depending on conditions and individual ability.Before the aircraft were submerged, an environmental impact assessment was conducted to identify potential risks associated with the operation. Reporting by Maldives Media TV said the assessment highlighted safety concerns for workers and seafarers and recommended precautions during the process. The project’s organisers also aimed to minimise ecological impacts while creating a new marine tourism attraction.Coral restoration brings a new phaseThe project entered a new phase on May 14, 2026, when Visit Maldives Corporation, HDC and Public Service Media (PSM) organised a large-scale coral restoration activity at the wreck site as part of the Asia Media Summit 2026, hosted by PSM. Around 300 international media delegates from 40 countries participated in the activity. They attached coral fragments to specially designed underwater frames, which were subsequently placed at the Dhoonier Wreck site as part of continuing restoration work. The activity also received support from government institutions, tourism businesses, dive operators and marine research organisations.According to Visit Maldives Corporation, the wreck project is a regenerative tourism initiative designed to combine marine restoration with diving experiences. Rather than treating the aircraft solely as submerged attractions, the long-term plan is to integrate them into a wider underwater habitat supported by coral planting and other habitat-enhancement efforts.The underwater layout is also planned around an airport-inspired design, with the aircraft forming structural elements within the developing reef environment. The coral-restoration activity is intended to help establish the site as both a distinctive diving destination and a setting for marine regeneration.However, the planting activity should not be confused with proof that a mature reef has already formed. Coral fragments need time to survive, grow and establish themselves, and the project's longer-term ecological results will depend on conditions at the site and continued monitoring.Can a sunken aircraft become an artificial reef?Artificial reefs are submerged structures that can provide surfaces for marine organisms to settle on and, under suitable conditions, create additional habitat for marine life. As corals and other organisms colonise a structure, it can become part of a more complex underwater environment.At Kudagiri, the aircraft provide the physical framework, while the coral-restoration programme is intended to encourage the development of a marine habitat around them. The approach offers a way to combine a tourism attraction with conservation work, although the extent of any ecological benefits will need to be established through observations over time.The Maldives is particularly associated with marine tourism, with coral reefs forming an important part of its underwater landscapes. A wreck-based attraction offers divers a different experience from conventional reef excursions, while the addition of coral restoration introduces a conservation component to the project.The Dhoonier Wreck also gives visitors a connection to the country's aviation past. The aircraft that once operated above the islands now offer a different kind of journey, allowing divers to explore their structure underwater while the restoration project progresses around them.Tourism and conservation beneath the wavesThe project reflects an effort to broaden the Maldives' tourism offerings beyond its established beach and resort experiences. The country's tourism authorities have presented the wreck as a destination that brings together underwater exploration, aviation heritage and environmental restoration.Its longer-term success, however, will depend on more than attracting visitors or completing coral planting. Establishing a healthy reef requires the transplanted coral to survive and grow, while the site must be managed to limit damage from diving activity and other disturbances. Continued ecological monitoring would help determine whether the restoration work is producing measurable benefits for marine life.For now, the two retired aircraft represent the starting point of an experiment in combining tourism infrastructure with reef restoration. The May 2026 activity marked a significant step in that effort, bringing coral planting directly to the wreck site. Whether the structures eventually support a thriving marine ecosystem remains a question for future monitoring.What began as an unusual underwater attraction near Kudagiri Island is therefore developing into something more ambitious: a project seeking to turn a piece of the Maldives' aviation history into a lasting feature of its marine environment.

articles.title: Ukraine’s access to Starlink a decision for Elon Musk, Rubio says
articles.summary: US secretary of state says White House not to blame for reported speed limits on internet services in Ukraine.
articles.body:
United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio says decisions about Ukraine’s access to Starlink are in the hands of its parent company, SpaceX, and CEO Elon Musk, not the White House, in response to claims it was involved in restricting Kyiv’s access to satellite internet services.

Rubio’s comments on Wednesday may increase scrutiny of US decision-making to potentially throttle the high-tech system, which allows Kyiv to intercept incoming projectiles and target Russian launchers.

The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday that Musk had ordered a slowdown of Starshield, a military-grade version of Starlink that Ukraine relies on for defence against Russian missile attacks.

The Journal quoted one person as saying Musk, US President Donald Trump and White House officials discussed the matter beforehand and two people as saying Musk and the president discussed the matter in the days after the slowdown.

The Reuters news agency has quoted two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter as saying the decision ultimately came from the White House.

This version was also confirmed by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy but denied by the Trump administration.

Zelenskyy adviser Serhii Beskrestnov wrote on the Telegram messaging app on October 14 that SpaceX had imposed a limit of 160 kilometres per hour (100 miles per hour) on Starshield services. That affected guidance systems for drones that Ukraine uses to intercept Russian drones flying at far greater speeds.

“Our defence forces received no prior warning regarding this restriction, and it has led to the disruption of a number of missions,” Beskrestnov said.

Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence confirmed the resumption of services on October 15.

Rubio told reporters during a trip to India on Wednesday that he was not aware if the administration knew about the decision beforehand but said it was “irrelevant”.

“The bottom line is that that is governed by a private commercial contract as to how their stuff can be used and what speeds they’ll allow it to be used at,” he said.

Musk had previously said on X that “any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS (President of the United States).”

Trump, asked by reporters on Wednesday whether Musk ordered the slowdown, said he did not know who did it but “I was not involved.”

Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth on Tuesday also portrayed the Starlink cutoff as a commercial matter.

“There are terms of service that ultimately need to be complied to, and that’s where Starlink has the option to make those decisions,” he said.

One significant point of confusion relates to the difference between SpaceX’s Starshield and Starlink products. Starshield is essentially a military-grade version of Starlink developed for the Pentagon.

Rubio suggested on Saturday that Ukraine never had access to Starshield while Zelenskyy has said both services had been disrupted in Ukraine.
