articles.title: Meet Isabel Rossi, a Williamsburg, Virginia eighth-grader who tested a new way to position earthquake sensors; her mathematical model improved simulated coverage by 16.7% with just five additional devices
articles.summary: A 14-year-old student from Williamsburg, Virginia, has earned her a place among 30 finalists in the 2026 Thermo Fisher Scientific Junior Innovators
articles.body: A 14-year-old student from Williamsburg, Virginia, has earned her a place among 30 finalists in the 2026 Thermo Fisher Scientific Junior Innovators Challenge for finding a new way to position earthquake sensors.Earthquake sensors can help detect seismic activity and provide early warnings, but deciding where to install them is not easy. Scientists must consider how accurately the devices can detect earthquakes, how much ground they can cover and whether their locations are accessible.According to The Virginian Pilot, Isabel Rossi, who carried out the research as an eighth-grader, developed a computer-based model that showed a possible 16.7% improvement in earthquake detection coverage using just five additional sensors.The finding emerged from a six-month project in which Isabel examined whether mathematical methods commonly used to make decisions could help identify better locations for earthquake sensors. For this, she worked with existing earthquake records and computer-generated sensor arrangements.Nearly 10,000 students applied to the national competition, which recognises research projects completed by middle school students across the United States. Isabel developed her project independently while attending James Blair Middle School. She is currently a freshman at Jamestown High School.According to Society for Science, which organises the challenge, Isabel's project, titled Listening in the Right Places: Game Theory and Optimisation for Earthquake Sensor Placement, was based on simulations.Importance of choosing sensor locations Earthquake monitoring depends on instruments that record seismic waves travelling through the ground. Some of these waves can be detected before stronger shaking reaches an area, allowing early warning systems to issue alerts. However, the usefulness of a sensor network also depends on where its instruments are located.For her study, Isabel concentrated on the Los Angeles region of California. She accessed a data library containing information about previous earthquakes and the locations of existing sensors. This allowed her to examine different arrangements without physically moving or installing any equipment.She wrote a computer program that generated random sets of possible sensor locations. Each arrangement was then assessed using two mathematical methods: a weighted sum model and Nash bargaining.The weighted sum model evaluates several objectives by assigning different levels of importance to them. Nash bargaining, a concept associated with game theory, looks for solutions that balance competing interests. Isabel used these approaches to examine the relationship between earthquake detection accuracy and sensor accessibility.The idea came after she read an article in Physics Today about the difficulties involved in detecting earthquakes. Having experienced a major earthquake herself, Isabel was already interested in the subject.What did the experiment find?Isabel compared their proposed sensor arrangements against the Pareto frontier, a mathematical concept used to identify solutions where improving one objective would mean making another worse.She examined whether an arrangement could provide better earthquake coverage without sacrificing another consideration, such as accessibility.Nash bargaining performed better in this comparison, producing arrangements closer to the Pareto frontier. Also, one model indicated that adding five sensors could improve simulated coverage by 16.7%.The finding does not establish that the same improvement would occur in an operational earthquake monitoring network. It does, however, show how mathematical modelling could help researchers compare possible sensor locations before making installation decisions.Isabel believes such methods could be particularly useful in places where reaching sensor locations is difficult or resources are limited.Isabel's love for mathematicsIsabel enjoys working through equations and mathematical proofs in her spare time and has described the precision of mathematics as one of its main attractions.“I like the precision of it. Over time it’s become one of my favorite free time activities," she told Society for Science.Her interest in scientific experiments began during childhood. Her father, Enrico Rossi, teaches physics at William & Mary, while her mother, Margarita Marinova, is an English professor at Christopher Newport University. Isabel also grew up watching her older sister Eleanor use chemistry and physics experiment sets.At nine, she began meeting a retired NASA engineer introduced to her by a teacher. Their activities included building homemade rockets, measuring their launches and making adjustments to improve their performance.She later organised a MathCounts team at James Blair Middle School and helped arrange a STEAM event to encourage younger students to explore science and mathematics. She continues to coach the mathematics team.Isabel also plays violin in the Williamsburg Youth Orchestra and participates in environmental science activities. She has expressed interest in careers involving aerospace engineering, applied mathematics or medicine.The national competition's final round will take place in Washington, DC, from October 23 to 28, bringing together students from 17 states and Puerto Rico. Finalists will compete for more than $100,000 in awards, including a $25,000 grand prize.

articles.title: Shamonda virus detected in human for first time in France; patient dies
articles.summary: French health authorities have detected the Shamonda virus, which primarily affects livestock, in a human for the first time.
articles.body: French health authorities have detected the Shamonda virus, which primarily affects livestock, in a human for the first time.The patient, who was severely immunocompromised and receiving treatment for a serious illness, died in Lyon in early October, authorities said.There is currently no identified health risk to the general population, according to the French authorities. Investigations into the case are continuing.The French agriculture ministry said the case was an exceptional one involving a severely immunocompromised patient. Until now, the virus had been considered non-transmissible to humans.According to investigations conducted so far, the patient’s brain complications before death were very likely linked to the Shamonda virus infection, the ministry said.How the patient may have contracted the virusThe leading hypothesis is that the patient was infected through an insect bite in eastern France, where the virus had been circulating among animals during the spring and summer of 2026.The suspected carrier is the Culicoides midge, a tiny biting insect known to transmit the virus.However, the circumstances of the infection are still being investigated.Clinical, laboratory and epidemiological investigations are ongoing. French authorities are also in contact with the World Health Organization (WHO) and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC), according to the ministry.What is the Shamonda virus?The Shamonda virus is an insect-borne virus belonging to the Orthobunyavirus group. It is primarily associated with livestock, particularly cattle, and is transmitted by biting midges.The virus was first identified in Nigeria in the mid-1960s. Since then, it has been detected sporadically in animals across parts of Africa and in Japan.In cattle, infection can cause fever, lethargy and diarrhoea. Dairy cows may also experience a significant decline in milk production, according to Belgium’s national public health institute, Sciensano.Although cattle are considered the main animal hosts, infections have also been reported in small ruminants and horses in France, according to Euronews.Virus detected in Europe this yearThe Shamonda virus was detected in Western Europe for the first time this summer, with cases reported in southern Germany, Switzerland, France and the Netherlands.The virus had previously been known to affect animals, and the French case marks the first documented detection in a human.French authorities said no health risk to the general population had been identified based on current knowledge of the virus.Investigations are continuing to establish the circumstances of the infection and its link to the patient’s illness.

articles.title: In a Hawaii coral experiment published in October 2026, scientists put an underwater speaker beside 3D-printed structures and bacteria-coated concrete blocks; coral larvae settled on coated blocks but not bare controls
articles.summary: A reef may be built from concrete and carefully engineered structures, but for young marine life, it appears that the right soundtrack could matter too.
articles.body: A reef may be built from concrete and carefully engineered structures, but for young marine life, it appears that the right soundtrack could matter too. In Hawaiʻi, scientists have been experimenting with an unusual approach to reef restoration, playing the sounds of a healthy coral reef underwater and combining them with artificial structures designed to provide the biological cues young corals need to settle. The results offer an intriguing new direction for rebuilding damaged reefs, although researchers stress that attracting larvae is only an early step toward creating a functioning ecosystem.Turning up the reef soundsAccording to Nature, the experiment took place in Kāneʻohe Bay, off Oʻahu, where researchers placed 37 artificial structures on a sandy seafloor at depths of about 4.5 metres. An underwater speaker played recordings captured from a healthy reef from sunset through sunrise for two weeks.The recordings contained the familiar crackles and pops produced by reef organisms, including fish and snapping shrimp. Healthy reefs tend to be noisier than degraded ones, where declining animal populations can leave the underwater environment comparatively quiet.Because coral and fish larvae drift through the ocean before choosing where to settle, these sounds can act as environmental clues. The researchers wanted to see whether restoring that acoustic signal could make artificial habitats more attractive.Adding bacteria to the equationSound was only one part of the experiment. Some of the artificial structures were coated with BRINK, a bioactive reef coating containing living bacteria.The idea comes from observations of natural reefs, where bacterial films on surfaces provide chemical cues that can help coral larvae identify suitable places to settle. By adding the living coating to artificial structures, researchers hoped to reproduce some of the signals normally found on healthy reef surfaces.The team conducted three experiments during coral spawning events in 2023 and 2024. Divers returned to the structures after the new moon and used specialised blue light and yellow filters to locate newly settled coral larvae.Sound and surface worked togetherThe strongest coral settlement occurred on structures positioned closest to the underwater speaker. The bacteria-coated structures performed particularly well, suggesting that combining acoustic and biological cues may be more effective than relying on an artificial surface alone.Some structures featuring crevices also performed well alongside the sound. Separately, 3D-printed structures developed by the Hawaiʻi Institute of Marine Biology showed promising results when exposed to reef sounds.A companion fish study found a similarly striking response. Autonomous underwater cameras recorded fish larvae for up to three weeks at sites with either an active or silent speaker. The sound-enhanced site attracted between four and 14 times more fish larvae overall, with the pattern remaining after researchers switched the locations of the speakers.A promising beginning, not a finished reefThe findings are encouraging, but they do not yet demonstrate that the approach can create a mature reef. The experiments measured settlement and larval abundance rather than whether the young organisms survived, grew into adults or ultimately established a functioning ecosystem.The fish results also represent a range rather than a single increase, and the experiments have so far been conducted at one location. Longer studies and trials at other reefs and during different seasons will be needed to determine whether the effect holds.The research forms part of a larger effort to develop hybrid reefs combining engineered structures with living coral. A planned project off Oʻahu could eventually put the concept into a much larger coastal-protection setting.Images Courtesy: istockFor now, the experiments suggest that reef restoration may involve more than providing a physical place to grow. Giving young marine life the right biological and acoustic signals could help guide them home.

articles.title: Amazon has lost 240 million acres of primary forest, about 15% of its original cover, a new study says; 32.2 million acres disappeared between 2022 and 2025, threatening vital rain-carrying pathways
articles.summary: Imagine Texas and California pushed together into one patch of land. Now picture all of it cut down, burned or otherwise gone.
articles.body: Imagine Texas and California pushed together into one patch of land. Now picture all of it cut down, burned or otherwise gone. That is roughly the amount of original primary forest the Amazon has lost, according to a new report from Amazon Conservation’s Monitoring of the Andes Amazon Program (MAAP). The latest analysis found that 97 million hectares (240 million acres) of primary forest had been lost across the Amazon biome’s nine countries by the end of 2025. It also found that the routes carrying moisture during the dry and transition seasons had been the most disrupted. Most of that loss came from people clearing land, with fire accounting for a large share. About 15% of the basin’s original forest is now gone.The numbers come from MAAP #250, a 2026 update to the group’s earlier tracking. In 2021, the same group put the figure at 13.2%. The jump may look small on paper, but it covers a huge amount of ground.The Amazon’s vanishing forestBetween 2022 and 2025 alone, another 13.04 million hectares (32.2 million acres) disappeared, the analysis found. That is nearly 15 times the size of Yellowstone National Park! According to the report, fire did much of the damage. The record fire losses of 2024 came after a strong El Niño season in 2023.This forest loss brings the Amazon closer to a tipping point which, according to scientific literature, could occur when about 25% of its forest is lost, alongside the effects of climate change. The pace of loss is crucial. A forest can take decades to recover, if it recovers at all, and every lost season pushes the basin closer to a point of no return.Rivers in the skyMost people never see the Amazon’s most important water system because it flies overhead. That’s right! Trees pull water up from the soil and release it into the air as vapour. Winds carry that moisture across the continent, and the forest recycles it again and again. The rainforest produces roughly half of its own rainfall, and that moisture may be reused up to six times as it moves. Scientists call these moving bands of moisture flying rivers.The MAAP analysis also broke down forest loss along the Amazon’s seasonal flying rivers. It found that some of these routes are weakening faster than others. The report found that moisture pathways during the dry and transition seasons have lost nearly three times as much forest as those during the wet season. These pathways are vital to forests in southwestern Amazonia, particularly in Peru and Bolivia, where forests recycle moisture that supplies more than 70% of rainfall across the basin. The wet-season route crosses thick, well-protected forest in the north and has lost only 3.2% of its forest connection. The routes active during the transition and dry seasons have lost nearly three times as much, at 9.1% and 8.6%, respectively. Brazil accounts for 79.4% of total forest loss. Bolivia comes next at 6.2%, followed by Peru at 5.8% and Colombia at 4.5%. Bolivia has climbed to second place from fourth in the 2022 assessment.These findings are especially concerning as a strong El Niño is forecast for late 2026. It could disrupt moisture flows during the wet season, extend dry periods and increase the risk of forest fires. The areas at greatest risk are the same regions where the report found the most damage to moisture pathways.“Media reports often indicate in general terms that the Amazon is approaching a tipping point, but this is the actual data indicating the magnitude of the problem. With 15% of the original Amazon lost to deforestation and fires, we are approaching the point at which the hydrological cycle that sustains rainforests may be permanently disrupted,” said Matt Finer, director of MAAP and senior research specialist at Amazon Conservation.Why the Amazon’s tipping point mattersThe Amazon’s tipping point hypothesis suggests that parts of the rainforest could shift towards drier savannah once about 25% of the forest is lost, especially if climate change disrupts rainfall and stretches the dry season. The Amazon is at roughly 15% now. That gap looks comfortable until you check how quickly the losses have piled up. Scientists believe this threshold is not a hard line. These changes may come gradually, in patches and unevenly across the basin. Some regions could feel the effects long before others.Meanwhile, a very strong El Niño is forecast to develop in late 2026. It could disrupt wet-season moisture flows, extend the dry season and raise the risk of fire, the researchers said. Those risks are greatest in the southwest, where the moisture routes have already suffered the most damage.For farmers and families in Peru and Bolivia who depend on that rain, the question is no longer about a distant tipping point. It is about whether the clouds keep coming.

articles.title: In 2017, bulldozers cleared Western Australian wetlands for a highway that was cancelled; nine years later, restoration has returned over 200,000 plants and recorded 97 animal species across 18 hectares
articles.summary: Nearly a decade after a controversial highway project damaged sensitive bushland in Western Australia, a long-running rehabilitation effort is showing
articles.body: Nearly a decade after a controversial highway project damaged sensitive bushland in Western Australia, a long-running rehabilitation effort is showing encouraging signs of ecological recovery, although restoring the landscape to its former condition remains a distant goal. According to a report by ABC News journalist Lauren Smith, a recent survey of the former Roe 8 highway corridor recorded 97 animal species across 18 hectares, alongside a substantial return of native vegetation. Information published by the City of Cockburn and the Western Australian government also outlines the continuing effort to rehabilitate the damaged land and protect the surrounding Beeliar Wetlands. Scroll down to read more…A highway project that left a lasting markThe Roe 8 extension was planned as part of the Perth Freight Link, a major road infrastructure proposal intended to improve freight access to Fremantle Port and ease congestion on surrounding roads. The project, however, became the focus of intense environmental opposition because its proposed route passed through ecologically sensitive bushland and wetlands.Preliminary work began in 2016, and land clearing escalated in early 2017. Conservationists warned that the destruction would damage habitats used by native wildlife, including Carnaby’s black cockatoos. The dispute drew protesters, environmental campaigners and government authorities into a prolonged confrontation over the future of the area.The political direction changed after the Labor Party won Western Australia’s state election in March 2017, suspending construction. Rehabilitation subsequently became a central part of efforts to address the environmental damage left behind. The state government formally closed the wider Roe 8 and Roe 9 Perth Freight Link project in January 2025, removing the road reservation that had allowed the proposed route to proceed.Native vegetation and wildlife returnThe rehabilitation programme, funded by Main Roads Western Australia and managed by the City of Cockburn, has focused on rebuilding vegetation and improving habitat across the cleared corridor. According to the latest survey results reported by ABC News, more than 4,300 animal detections were recorded, representing 97 different species. The survey also identified the return of several species to the area, including Carnaby’s black cockatoos and quendas, a small native marsupial also known as the southern brown bandicoot.More than 280,000 seedlings were planted during the earlier stages of rehabilitation. The programme has since seen native vegetation re-establish across the damaged land, with the number of plants estimated to have risen from virtually none in the cleared sections to more than 200,000.The findings suggest that sustained revegetation and habitat management can help degraded landscapes recover. However, the presence of wildlife and returning vegetation does not necessarily mean that the original ecosystem has been fully restored.Why recovery remains difficultRebuilding a natural landscape is more complicated than planting trees and shrubs. Some native species are difficult to propagate, while others depend on specific environmental conditions to establish themselves.Orchids, for example, must return naturally to the corridor rather than being planted as part of the restoration effort. The exposed ground also creates a hotter microclimate, making it harder for certain native plants to survive and grow. These challenges highlight the difference between restoring visible greenery and rebuilding a functioning ecosystem. The wetlands and surrounding bushland developed over long periods, supporting intricate relationships between vegetation, insects, birds and other wildlife that cannot be recreated overnight.The City of Cockburn’s rehabilitation programme follows a 10-year management plan covering the corridor’s different habitats, with monitoring and community participation forming important parts of the work.A long road aheadThe progress has offered encouragement to people who opposed the highway’s construction and later became involved in repairing the damaged landscape. Yet local officials have stressed that the recovery remains incomplete. Cockburn Mayor Logan Howlett has estimated that the bushland has returned to roughly 30 per cent of the condition it should eventually reach. The rehabilitation programme’s achievements therefore represent an important stage in a much longer process rather than a final measure of success.The programme is approaching the end of its original 10-year period, but local leaders want restoration work to continue beyond that milestone. Further monitoring, weed management, revegetation and protection of returning wildlife will remain important to the corridor’s future.The Roe 8 experience also leaves a broader lesson for environmental planning: the consequences of clearing established natural habitats can persist long after a development project has been abandoned. Although thousands of seedlings and the return of native animals demonstrate meaningful progress, recovering the ecological complexity of the original landscape may take generations.

articles.title: Sure, let’s smoosh SpaceX and Tesla together, who cares
articles.summary: SpaceX and Tesla may finally merge, and Elon Musk may get a pretty big payout from it. Is that really a good idea? I’m not sure it matters.
articles.body: Oh sure, SpaceX’s credit risk is pretty high because it’s about to borrow another $40 billion to spend on Nvidia chips, but who cares about that? SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees to discuss a merger! The degree to which you find this merger compelling likely has to do with the degree to which you believe Elon Musk about wanting to go to Mars, or “spread the light of consciousness,” as he put it in this week’s SpaceX earnings call (and earlier S-1). Now, a reasonably informed person knows that we don’t have the technology — or, frankly, even the raw information to build the technology — in order to support human life in space. So that means robots. But a lag between Earth and the Moon or Mars makes for difficulty in controlling the robots. So having artificially intelligent robots who can make decisions on their own with minimal supervision from Earth is the next sci-fi logic step. If you believe Musk’s story, the technology we are talking about is being developed through self-driving cars (Tesla), LLMs (SpaceX), and humanoid robots (Tesla), all of which require data centers (SpaceX). Conveniently, we have just had earnings for both companies. On the other hand, if you view Mars as a useful fiction Musk uses to explain his antics in public, well, there’s a lot of money and a lot of control Musk gets from the merger. Musk said on the recent SpaceX earnings call that “there’s a lot of merit to combining” SpaceX and Tesla. Why? “There’s a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software.” But artificial intelligence — ah, excuse me, super intelligence software isn’t the business SpaceX is really in right now. In its Q3 earnings on Tuesday, SpaceX reported $7.56 billion in revenue from the artificial intelligence — sorry, sorry, super intelligence division. The subcategory “SI solutions & infrastructure revenues” — which I think is Grok, Cursor, and the neocloud business wrapped together — jumped to $7 billion, or more than three times what it was last quarter. Now some of this was getting Cursor stapled on, which added $608 million in revenue. Most of the rest of that $7 billion was likely renting out compute to Anthropic and Google; Grok is probably contributing less, says Gil Luria, an analyst at DA Davidson. At first blush, this may look comparable to the revenue of a company like Anthropic, whose leaked S-1 shows the company had $16.3 billion in revenue in the first half of this year from its frontier models. But SpaceX’s AI business looks more like CoreWeave than Anthropic. While we are told in the press release there was “increased Grok adoption across enterprise customers and consumers,” that number wasn’t broken out from bare-metal revenue. And if Musk wanted to brag about it, he would. As for Tesla, which released Q3 results on Wednesday, its earnings sucked — a second consecutive quarter of declining profits. That’s because Musk is apparently not especially interested in normal cars anymore. Instead, Tesla is focusing on robots and, I guess, self-driving taxis. (There was also a Roadster hopping car demo recently, but that’s not going into production for a couple years, it’s very expensive, and Tesla cannot guarantee it will be delivered.) Musk did not elaborate on his comments about the merger on the Tesla call. Macroharder SpaceX and Tesla have some tie-ups already; SpaceX, for instance, bought $131 million of the low-selling Cybertrucks from Tesla. It has, in the past, held Tesla bonds. More crucially, the companies have also announced two AI — fuck it, we’re just sticking with AI — projects together: Terafab and Macrohard. Terafab is the chip-making venture that Musk intends to build in Texas and run to supply himself with chips; Intel is partnered, kinda, with Musk to develop the technology. Macrohard is, uh, an AI project that lets people simulate software already made by Microsoft. At least, I think that’s what it’s supposed to be. Typing the name of the latter makes me pray for the asteroid to hit us all right now, so perhaps it’s fortunate that we haven’t heard much about it since the announcement in March. SpaceX’s S-1 from May said that Terafab and Microhard “are in the very early stages, as a result of which we and Tesla have not finalized a variety of details relating to our collaboration, including, but not limited to, financial terms, intellectual property rights, and the ultimate term of our collaboration.” As of earlier this month, Intel’s CEO said the company remained committed to the partnership, but it’s not obligated to remain part of Terafab and the S-1 says there may never be a definitive agreement. Intel’s Thomas Hannaford didn’t immediately respond to my emails asking if anything had been signed in the interim. On this week’s call with SpaceX investors, Musk claimed the Terafab will reach volume production in the second half of 2028. He also said the company will have its first test chip from the facility in May or June 2027. “Musk has a history of setting timelines that his ​companies have missed,” Reuters notes, with a degree of what I can only describe as wry understatement. When an analyst on the call asked if Musk had placed orders for machines needed to make cutting-edge equipment, Musk did not answer. Companies often are doing more privately than they announce publicly, so I do not view the S-1 filing as fully definitive. But Macrohard isn’t mentioned in the last 10Q. Neither is Terafab. The Matt Levine case for the SpaceX-Tesla merger Musk is going to pound the table about the Moon, Mars, “and beyond,” and a significant chunk of his fan base is very into this. But there are maybe some boring financial reasons shareholders may have an interest. Let’s say you are constitutionally very different from me, and much richer, and for this reason you own a number of shares in Tesla. You’re a big believer in Elon Musk — obviously — but you notice that the man has an attention span of a squirrel on cocaine. He’s on X basically constantly and often racistly. He keeps showing up at the White House to do stuff that pisses off would-be Tesla customers. Then he publicly feuds with the president. Sometimes he’s very excited about rockets, and sometimes he’s very excited about Dogecoin and sometimes he’s really into Grok and sometimes he thinks about cars. But you notice that one way or the other he’s been thinking about cars a lot less lately. Since he seems to be focused — insofar as he can be said to focus — on AI, you notice some pretty big conflicts of interest. Musk’s companies “all need the same scarce Nvidia chips to power their AI, for instance,” notes Matt Levine, a longtime Musk observer. But if you combine the companies, well, maybe you build the best general-purpose AI. And then? “If you build the best general-purpose AI model, maybe it can drive the cars and operate the robots and upload people’s brains and serve right-wing takes on Twitter.” Also, there’s a massive AI infrastructure buildout happening, and so basically all you have to do is say “Nvidia” and someone will give you a fuckton of money. The merger puts all the AI projects in one pile, plus also some cars and rockets and satellites I guess. “‘Give us $100 billion to build data centers in space, but if for some reason we don’t build data centers in space you can repossess our car factories and data centers on earth’ is a good pitch to credit investors,” Levine writes. Musk also has a history — not always successful — of building physical infrastructure. This is, at least from my point of view, a better bet when it comes to building data centers than some Bitcoin miners who pivoted. “If Elon builds at the rate he talked about, he will have lots of extra capacity and be able to sell much of it,” says Luria. From this point of view, obviously SpaceX and Tesla should merge, Levine writes: > It’s crazy that they are separate companies! One guy runs two gigantic physical AI companies with huge overlaps! What a nightmare of conflicts of interest and red tape! Just merge them, so that the one guy can come into the office each day with a simple mandate: Make the choices that maximize overall value for the giant AI complex, and for the shareholders of that complex. If some chips or engineers or drills or whatever should be working on robots, work on the robots; if they should be working on data centers, work on the data centers. The shareholders have come this far; surely they trust Musk to make those decisions. It’s just that right now, working on the robots is good for Tesla and bad for SpaceX; working on the data centers is bad for Tesla and good for SpaceX. Musk can’t put both of their interests first. There’s an easy fix. It’s not exactly that simple, of course. The details of the deal matter; a lot of people are assuming a stock-for-stock merger. (“I assume the acquirer would be SpaceX, in part because it has a bigger market capitalization but mostly because of Musk’s greater control there,” Levine writes.) So does the regulatory environment. The case that SpaceX and Tesla should combine due to AI is also kind of an antitrust reason they shouldn’t? The current regulatory environment is, in large part due to Musk’s meddling via his DOGE cronies, let’s say lax. Donald Trump, the current president, has two more years left in his term. Also, the markets have started getting waves of nervousness around AI. Earlier this summer, there was the Situational Awareness thing, and then there was the more recent CoreWeave thing, and, well, investor sentiment may be changing. That means “there’s a push to announce a deal by the first half of 2027 so that it closes during this administration,” Bloomberg writes, attributing this to “people who are familiar with the matter.” Shares and shares alike Musk has more control at SpaceX than he does at Tesla. His voting power is above 50 percent, because he owns special supervoting shares. He is the CEO, CTO, and chairman of the board. Shareholders are very limited in how they can legally challenge that power. The filing puts it this way: “This will limit or preclude your ability to influence corporate matters and the election of our directors.” At Tesla, however, Musk only has about 20 percent of the vote. (“Only!”) So in a stock-for-stock merger, where SpaceX is the acquirer, Musk suddenly has voting control of the whole enchilada. “He gets voting control of Tesla in the only way he can,” says Ann Lipton, a professor at the University of Colorado Boulder’s law school. “He can’t change it to a dual-class entity now that it’s publicly traded. This is the only way to do it.” Both companies are based in Texas, which makes it very difficult for shareholders to sue, says Lipton. “The chances of a shareholder being able to sue on the Tesla or SpaceX side are vanishingly small because Texas has erected so many barriers to shareholder litigation.” So there’s that risk gone. Leave aside the more complicated issues of national security (for SpaceX) and antitrust. At a federal level, securities laws are largely “Did you disclose it?” notes Lipton. So the SEC, or what remains of it, will want to see that everything is disclosed to shareholders before the vote. As long as the disclosures are accurate, that’s that. At the state level, there may be some issues — it’s a breach of fiduciary duty to create an unfair transaction as a result of conflicts of interest — but Shari Redstone did merge Paramount and CBS, so it’s not impossible. What does Musk get from this merger? Well, control, a thing he historically loves most of all. Potentially also, the combination adds $110 billion to his net worth, according to Bloomberg. More interesting, however, is how the merger interacts with Musk’s massive Tesla compensation package. If there’s a legal change of control — for instance, because SpaceX buys Tesla — the operational milestones in Musk’s enormous pay package fall away. What matters then is Tesla’s valuation. If SpaceX pays $2 trillion or more, Musk gets a payout. At $2 trillion, Musk gets $6 billion of shares. He also gets accelerated vesting of shares from his 2018 pay package — which would otherwise have vested in 2028. The change of control also means he can sell them sooner. Is that good for SpaceX? Assuming we wind up at or around the $2 trillion figure, we’re looking at basically a merger of equals — which means current SpaceX shareholders get diluted all to hell. Worse, Tesla’s business is stagnating, and its AI ambitions are expensive. “It’s likely that SpaceX and Tesla combined will spend close to a staggering $50 billion on capex in Q4, and their businesses won’t come close to covering that number,” writes Shawn Tully in Fortune. So on a numbers basis, I kind of think no, not really, not that good for SpaceX. But none of Musk’s businesses are about numbers in the end — they are, to some extent, about how much you believe in Elon Musk. That’s what the Tesla valuation versus regular automakers was about in the first place. So sure, fine, slap them together and see what happens. The people who are buying what Musk’s selling, at this point, surely know what they signed up for.

articles.title: After invasive rats were eliminated from a Pacific island in 2005, scientists monitored seabirds for years; three species eventually recorded populations two to ten times larger than before the removal
articles.summary: A Pacific island has recorded a significant recovery in several seabird populations following the removal of invasive rats in 2005.
articles.body: A Pacific island has recorded a significant recovery in several seabird populations following the removal of invasive rats in 2005. A study published in Conservation Biology examined how seven seabird species responded after rodents were eradicated from Surprise Island in New Caledonia. According to the researchers, three species experienced substantial population increases, with their breeding populations eventually reaching between two and ten times their earlier levels. The findings also revealed that recovery did not happen immediately for every species. While some seabirds increased within a few years, others showed improvements only after longer periods of monitoring, highlighting the importance of sustained conservation efforts.Why invasive rats threatened seabirdsSurprise Island is a small, uninhabited island in the Pacific, covering approximately 24 hectares. Before the eradication programme, it was home to invasive black rats and house mice, which posed a threat to nesting seabirds. Rodents can prey on eggs and chicks, reducing the number of young birds that survive to adulthood. On islands where seabirds nest on the ground or in accessible locations, these introduced predators can have particularly damaging effects. Native birds may have evolved without such predators and may lack effective defences against them.In 2005, conservationists eliminated the invasive rodents from Surprise Island. The eradication was confirmed as successful in 2006. Researchers subsequently examined whether removing the predators helped seabird populations recover and whether the benefits differed between species.Scientists tracked seven seabird speciesThe research team monitored seven seabird species, including red-footed boobies, brown boobies, masked boobies, noddies and frigatebirds. Their analysis combined surveys conducted before and after the eradication with observations collected over subsequent years. Annual surveys between 2002 and 2009 provided information about breeding populations before and shortly after the rodents were removed. Researchers also used earlier observations from 1995 and 1996 and later surveys conducted between 2017 and 2021.Rather than simply counting birds flying over the island, the team recorded active nests containing adults, eggs or chicks to estimate the number of breeding pairs. This approach helped them assess whether the seabirds were establishing and maintaining breeding populations. The extended monitoring period was particularly important because population changes were not equally visible across all species. Some responded relatively quickly, while others took considerably longer to show clear signs of recovery.Noddies and frigatebirds increased after eradicationNoddies and frigatebirds were among the species that showed relatively early improvements after the invasive rodents disappeared. Their breeding populations increased within four years of eradication, suggesting that the island had become a more favourable place for nesting. The long-term results for noddies were especially striking. Researchers estimated that the island supported around 400 breeding pairs in 1995. By 2021, the estimated number had reached 5,346 pairs, representing approximately a tenfold increase.Frigatebirds also experienced substantial growth. Researchers recorded 1,586 breeding pairs in October 2017, compared with 398 pairs estimated in December 1996. The researchers suggested that birds arriving from nearby islands may have contributed to these increases. With invasive rodents no longer threatening their eggs and chicks, Surprise Island could provide safer nesting opportunities for seabirds looking to establish new breeding sites.Red-footed boobies showed delayed recoveryRed-footed boobies responded differently. During the first four years after eradication, researchers did not observe a clear increase in their breeding population. This showed why short-term surveys alone may not provide a complete picture of the effects of conservation work. Later observations revealed stronger growth. The estimated number of breeding pairs reached 4,698 in 2017 and 5,548 in 2019, before declining to 3,256 in 2021. Before the rodents were removed, the estimated population had never exceeded 2,883 pairs.The delayed increase may be linked to the birds’ breeding biology. Long-lived seabirds often take several years to mature, so improvements in breeding success may take time to translate into a larger adult population. However, not every species showed a clear long-term increase. Brown and masked boobies did not experience the same measurable recovery, indicating that removing invasive predators does not guarantee identical results for all seabirds.Long-term monitoring reveals conservation benefitsThe study provides evidence that eliminating invasive rodents can help support the recovery of island seabird populations, but the results may take years to become fully apparent. Noddies and frigatebirds showed relatively early improvements, while red-footed boobies required longer monitoring before their population increases became clear.The researchers’ findings also highlight the importance of evaluating individual species rather than assuming that an entire seabird community will respond in the same way. Differences in breeding behaviour, survival and movement between islands can influence recovery.Surprise Island provides an example of how targeted conservation efforts can benefit wildlife after an invasive threat has been removed. The research also underlines why long-term surveys are essential for determining whether those gains continue and for identifying species that may need additional protection.

articles.title: Colorado built a wildlife overpass across a busy highway; a new report says animal-vehicle collisions fell by 91% as elk, bears and frogs began using the crossing
articles.summary: For wildlife, a busy highway can be more than an obstacle.
articles.body: For wildlife, a busy highway can be more than an obstacle. It can separate feeding grounds, disrupt seasonal migrations and turn an ordinary journey into a deadly gamble. In Colorado, a new network of wildlife crossings is helping change that equation, with officials reporting a sharp decline in collisions along a heavily travelled stretch of Interstate 25. Reporting by Smithsonian Magazine, Colorado Politics and The Colorado Sun has highlighted the results of the state’s wildlife mitigation programme, which combines fencing, underpasses and a recently completed overpass near Monument. The findings suggest that infrastructure designed around animal movement can make roads safer for wildlife while reducing risks for motorists.A highway that divided wildlife habitatInterstate 25 is one of Colorado’s major transport routes, connecting communities along the state’s Front Range. The stretch between Castle Rock and Monument carries more than 100,000 vehicles a day and cuts through extensive wildlife habitat, creating a dangerous barrier for animals that need to move between seasonal ranges. Elk, mule deer and pronghorn travel between lower elevations in winter and mountain habitats in summer. When their routes intersect with fast-moving traffic, the consequences can be devastating for animals and drivers alike.To address the problem, agencies began developing a wildlife crossing system in 1996. The programme eventually included about 14 miles of fencing on both sides of the highway and five underpasses designed to guide animals beneath traffic. The latest addition is a $15 million wildlife overpass near Monument, which opened in December 2025. Measuring approximately 200 feet wide and 209 feet long, the structure spans six lanes of traffic and covers roughly 41,800 square feet. State officials describe it as the largest wildlife overpass of its kind in North America.Collision numbers show a dramatic declineThe results have been striking. According to figures reported by Colorado Politics, wildlife-vehicle collisions along the 18-mile corridor fell by approximately 85 per cent annually between 2022 and 2024, after most of the mitigation infrastructure had been completed. During the final year covered by the study, collisions were down 91 per cent.The distinction matters: the reduction reflects the combined crossing system, rather than the overpass alone. Officials are continuing to collect data to determine the bridge’s individual contribution to the improvement. The Colorado Sun has also reported that only two wildlife-related crashes had been recorded since the overpass opened, although that early figure does not by itself establish the long-term impact of the structure. The benefits extend to traffic flow. Fewer collisions mean fewer emergency responses, damaged vehicles and unexpected delays on a busy commuter and freight route.From elk to frogs, animals are using the bridgeTrail cameras and wildlife surveys have recorded a range of animals using the crossing system. Elk have been photographed crossing the new bridge, while pronghorn have begun moving to areas west of I-25 after decades of limited safe passage.Smaller creatures are benefiting, too. Reports have documented rabbits and northern leopard frogs using the overpass. Designers have also placed logs along parts of the crossing to give small mammals, including the threatened Preble’s meadow jumping mouse, additional cover from predators.Vegetation is another important part of the plan. Drought conditions have slowed plant growth on the bridge, and officials hope improved vegetation will make the crossing more attractive to wildlife as the habitat develops. The goal is not simply to get animals over the road. It is to create a passage that feels safe and familiar enough for different species to use as part of their natural movements.Colorado plans more wildlife crossingsThe success of the I-25 project is informing wider efforts to reduce collisions across Colorado. Officials are developing six additional crossing systems, including an overpass specifically designed for Rocky Mountain bighorn sheep, the state’s official animal.Wildlife crossings require substantial upfront investment, but preventing collisions can also reduce the economic costs associated with vehicle damage, injuries, emergency services and traffic disruption. Colorado’s experience demonstrates why conservation infrastructure is increasingly being considered alongside traditional road safety measures. Fencing directs animals towards designated routes, underpasses provide alternatives beneath traffic, and overpasses reconnect habitats that highways have divided.The latest figures offer encouraging evidence that these measures can work when planned as a connected system. For Colorado, the challenge now is to sustain the improvements, monitor how animals use the crossings over time and determine where similar infrastructure could make the greatest difference. A highway may remain essential for people travelling through the state, but it no longer has to be an insurmountable barrier for the wildlife living alongside it.

articles.title: SpaceX in Talks to Access 80,000 Cell Sites for Wireless Network
articles.summary: SpaceX aims to secure a minimum of 80,000 cell sites across the US, and it’s in talks with at least one major cellular infrastructure company to reach that g...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- SpaceX aims to secure a minimum of 80,000 cell sites across the US, and it's in talks with at least one major cellular infrastructure company to reach that goal, according to people familiar with the matter.

The agreements would solidify the rocket and satellite giant's path toward building a fourth nationwide wireless carrier, said the people, who asked to not be identified because the discussions are private. One of the companies they're in talks with is Crown Castle Inc., which, along with American Tower Corp. and Vertical Bridge Holdings, are among the largest owners of cellular towers.

When asked on a Wednesday earnings conference call whether Crown Castle is discussing leases with SpaceX, Amazon.com Inc. or other satellite-based telecom providers, Chief Executive Officer Chris Hillabrant said, "You can assume that we're talking to all parties." He declined to discuss specific customer details.

American Tower declined to comment. SpaceX and Vertical Bridge didn't immediately respond to requests for comment.

Mobile networks rely on antennas placed on towers across the country to transmit wireless signals. Carriers such as AT&T Inc., Verizon Communications Inc. and T-Mobile US Inc. typically lease room for their equipment at the tower sites because it's more cost effective than owning and maintaining them, in part because the facilities can be shared.

The value of the deals with SpaceX could reach into the billions.

SpaceX Chief Executive Officer Elon Musk has made no secret of his intentions to create a standalone wireless carrier from scratch, threatening the existing dominant providers with increased competition from a well-funded and politically potent new rival. While the prospect requires significant investment, Musk is plowing ahead.

SpaceX recently acquired low-band spectrum that will help it parlay its Starlink satellites and other elements into what Musk described as a "major mobile carrier." The company won Federal Communications Commission approval to launch 15,000 satellites designed to provide mobile service directly to phones. Wireless tower sites are another key component that SpaceX must assemble to establish reliable links with users on the ground.

articles.title: A novel mRNA cancer vaccine helps reduce the chances of melanoma patients' tumors returning

articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A first-of-its-kind cancer vaccine is significantly reducing the chances that melanoma patients' tumors come back, according to results of a major study released Thursday by drugmakers Moderna and Merck.

The vaccine was custom-brewed for each patient to match their tumor. Adding it to a standard post-surgery treatment reduced by 42% the risk of melanoma returning two years after surgery, according to the most advanced study to date of this new strategy for fighting cancer.

"The field has been looking for a win and I think this one is a big one," said Dr. Hussein Tawbi of MD Anderson Cancer Center in Houston, one of the researchers in the international study.

The vaccine, called intismeran, is made with the same Nobel Prize-winning mRNA technology that was behind COVID-19 vaccines. Experimental personalized cancer vaccines made with mRNA and some other approaches also are being tested against other types of cancer including lung, kidney and pancreatic.

Experts not involved with the new study say its success bolsters the field.

"This is a new frontier," said Karen Knudsen, CEO of the Parker Institute, which helps fund cancer immunotherapy research.

"It's a big step forward for science, for oncology, because this vaccine will apply to many different cancers," said Dr. Michael Atkins, deputy director of Georgetown University's Lombardi Comprehensive Cancer Center.

Moderna and Merck had announced in August that the late-stage trial of intismeran was successful but the detailed results were set to be released Saturday at a meeting of the European Society of Medical Oncology in Madrid. Some of the data was leaked publicly late Thursday, prompting a full release ahead of the weekend's scientific presentation.

Most people think of vaccines as preventing an infection, like measles or whooping cough. There are already two cancer-preventing vaccines, the HPV and hepatitis B shots that block infection from those tumor-causing viruses. And research is underway to prevent some types of inherited cancer such as Lynch syndrome-caused colorectal cancer.

But a personalized vaccine designed to block surgically-removed cancer from returning is very different. For the intismeran study, scientists hunted gene mutations unique to each patient's tumor, mutations that create proteins which shouldn't be in the body unless those cancer cells start to grow again. The custom vaccine — nine doses given three weeks apart — teaches the patient's immune system to watch out for and attack those so-called neoantigens.

How did it work? The study included more than 1,100 people with high-risk melanoma that was surgically removed. Everyone was given the standard follow-up therapy: Merck's immunotherapy named Keytruda. The participants were randomly assigned to also receive custom-brewed vaccine doses or a placebo.

Two years later, 82% of the people in the vaccine group were still living without a recurrence of their cancer compared to 70% who had gotten standard Keytruda alone. The trial is continuing to track participants' longer-term outcomes.

In 2024, Tony Hout joined the vaccine trial at MD Anderson after seeking care for a spot on his ear that had been bleeding intermittently and wouldn't fully heal. Doctors recognized melanoma and during surgery discovered it had started to spread.

"I want to make sure I'm doing everything I can to be here for my family," said Hout, 62, who has since moved to Cayuga, Indiana, and travels back to Houston every few months for a study check-up. Scans this week showed he's still cancer-free.

The vaccine's side effects were mainly the sore arm, fatigue and other reactions typical of mRNA coronavirus vaccination, MD Anderson's Tawbi said.

Moderna and Merck are talking with regulatory authorities about next steps for seeking approval of the vaccine.

Customized medicines generally are very expensive. The drugmakers aren't discussing what such a cancer vaccine might cost.

But Moderna President Stephen Hoge said the company's special cancer vaccine manufacturing facility in Massachusetts is providing doses for thousands of people enrolled in multiple studies underway internationally.

Hoge said it takes a few days to brew the vaccine but the whole process, starting with analyzing the tumor genetics to come up with what is essentially a recipe for each patient, can take roughly six weeks, sometimes more. Meanwhile, the melanoma patients had already started their standard Keytruda, a different kind of immunotherapy.

Moderna shares dropped 18% Thursday after the study's full results were made public, but they remained more than 200% higher than they were in late August before investors were first told of the initial results.

articles.body: A centuries-old archaeological puzzle at Westminster Abbey in London may finally be nearing a resolution, with new research suggesting that a skeleton discovered inside a Roman stone coffin belonged to a medieval abbot rather than the Roman-era man named on its inscription. According to an announcement by Westminster Abbey and reports by The Guardian and Live Science published on October 21, 2026, archaeologists have identified two possible candidates for the burial, with one emerging as the likelier match. The limestone sarcophagus was officially excavated in 1869, although it had reportedly been uncovered during building work decades earlier. Its inscription commemorates Valerius Amandinus, a wealthy Briton who lived during the fourth century. However, a large Christian cross carved into the lid belongs to a much later period, raising questions about when the coffin was reused and who was eventually buried inside it.A Roman coffin with a medieval secretThe contrast between the inscription and the cross provided an early clue that the sarcophagus had served more than one purpose. While its original construction dates to the Roman period, the cross was carved during the late Anglo-Saxon era, around the 10th or 11th century. The coffin had also suffered damage and was reportedly looted before its contents could be properly investigated. For years, researchers believed the skeleton might no longer survive. That assumption changed in 2016, when the sarcophagus was opened at a conservation studio and an almost complete human skeleton was discovered inside. The remains were subsequently examined by specialists, including human bone expert James Young Langthorne of Pre-Construct Archaeology. Their findings, discussed in a new study by Westminster Abbey’s consulting archaeologist, Warwick Rodwell, have helped establish the burial’s likely date and the status of the individual.What the skeleton revealedAnalysis indicated that the remains belonged to a man who was approximately 35 to 49 years old and around 5 feet 9 inches tall. Examination of the bones also identified signs of osteoarthritis, gout and two healed rib fractures. Radiocarbon dating placed the man’s remains between AD 987 and 1052, firmly establishing that he lived centuries after the Roman sarcophagus was made. The results support the conclusion that the coffin was repurposed during the late Anglo-Saxon period.Researchers also identified traces of a rectangular structure inside the stone coffin, marked by a white residue associated with lime. Rodwell’s analysis suggests that the deceased was originally placed in a wooden coffin inside the much older stone sarcophagus. The wooden structure eventually decayed, leaving behind evidence of its former outline. The reuse of an elaborate Roman burial container for a medieval religious figure may also help explain why the individual received such a substantial burial.Two abbots emerge as possible identitiesIn his study, published in the Journal of the British Archaeological Association, Rodwell narrowed the possible identities to two former leaders of Westminster’s Benedictine monastery: Ælfwig and his successor, Wulfnoth. Ælfwig served as abbot from 993 to around 1020, while Wulfnoth held the position from approximately 1020 until 1049. Both lived within the period indicated by the radiocarbon results and are considered plausible candidates for the burial.Ælfwig is regarded as the stronger possibility because he was already a monk at Westminster before becoming abbot. However, the available archaeological evidence does not establish the deceased’s identity beyond doubt, and Wulfnoth remains a viable alternative. The lack of surviving grave goods makes a definitive identification more difficult. Any objects that might once have accompanied the burial may have disappeared during the earlier disturbance of the tomb.A mystery preserved at Westminster AbbeyThe findings add another chapter to the history of a sarcophagus that has survived repeated discoveries, damage and conservation work. Investigations into the abbey’s former sacristy area, including archaeological work undertaken by Pre-Construct Archaeology, have helped researchers reconstruct the circumstances surrounding its burial and eventual rediscovery.Today, the sarcophagus is displayed in Westminster Abbey’s Queen’s Diamond Jubilee Galleries, where visitors can see the Roman inscription and the medieval cross that helped trigger the investigation. Although the identity of the man remains uncertain, the new research provides a clearer picture of his likely place in history: a high-ranking religious figure buried in an ancient stone coffin that had already survived several centuries before it was reused.
